Optimal Batching with Abandonment: Threshold Policies Under Risk-Neutral and Risk-Sensitive Criteria

Shuren Wang Affiliation: Rice University Email: sw79@rice.edu    Guodong Pang Affiliation: Rice University Email: gdpang@rice.edu
Abstract

We study optimal batching in a discrete-time Markovian system with Bernoulli arrivals and independent item abandonment. Each batch earns a per-item processing reward and incurs holding, abandonment, and fixed stopping costs. We formulate the batching decision as an optimal stopping problem and characterize optimal threshold policies under risk-neutral, risk-seeking, and risk-averse criteria. Under risk neutrality and the entropic risk-seeking criterion, the value function admits a forward-recursion representation, and the resulting reduced objectives are strictly unimodal. In the risk-seeking case, the objective is strictly discretely concave, yielding an explicit marginal-cost condition. For risk aversion, the unregularized entropic continuation branch may diverge, precluding standard fixed-point arguments. We therefore study a regularized robust surrogate formulated as a minimax problem with a relative-entropy penalty and capped likelihood ratio. We establish the existence of an optimal threshold policy and derive an explicit truncated-Gibbs worst-case distribution. We also study repeated batch clearing under both the long-run average and discounted criteria, for which the threshold objectives remain strictly unimodal. Numerical experiments examine threshold sensitivity to system parameters, costs, and risk preferences.

Keywords: Optimal stopping, Batch clearing, Abandonment, Risk-neutral and risk-sensitive control, Threshold policies, KL-regularized robust control, Repeated clearing

1 Introduction

The coordination of batch processing and inventory accumulation is a fundamental operational challenge. In manufacturing, components arriving from upstream stations are consolidated into batches before transfer to downstream lines (Deb and Serfozo 1973); in logistics, customer orders accumulate at distribution centers until a vehicle is dispatched (Çetinkaya and Lee 2002); in telecommunications, data packets are buffered until a transmission block is formed (Xiong et al. 2000); and in healthcare, platelet concentrates from multiple donations are pooled into transfusion doses, with production and inventory decisions coordinated to balance uncertain demand against outdating (Haijema et al. 2007). At the same time, when items accumulate in a system, they are typically subject to forces that reduce the inventory level over time. Customers waiting in a queue may abandon out of impatience (Baccelli and Hébuterne 1981, Garnett et al. 2002). Perishable goods in a cold chain may spoil (Graves 1982, Kaspi and Perry 1983, Nahmias 2011). Data packets in a router buffer may expire when their time-to-live counters reach zero. In each setting, processing items individually sacrifices economies of scale, whereas waiting to form larger batches increases holding costs and the risk that items leave the system before processing.

We study a discrete-time batch accumulation problem that captures this trade-off. Items arrive stochastically, at most one per period, and each waiting item independently abandons before processing at a constant per-period rate. At the beginning of each period, the decision maker either processes the accumulated batch—paying a fixed stopping cost and earning a per-item reward—or continues accumulating, incurring holding costs on the waiting items and a penalty on each item that abandons. We analyze the resulting optimal stopping problem under three criteria: a discounted risk-neutral criterion, an undiscounted risk-seeking entropic criterion, and a robustly regularized risk-averse criterion.

Existing methods do not directly cover this problem, for two reasons. First, in the classical clearing and batch-service models cited below, items are not lost one by one before clearing or service; here, abandonment destroys that cumulative structure, and the usual monotonicity/submodularity sufficient conditions for threshold optimality cannot be satisfied. Second, the risk-sensitive stopping results closest to our entropic criterion assume bounded running/terminal costs or comparable regularity, whereas here both grow linearly on an unbounded state space. Under risk aversion, the unregularized continuation branch lacks uniform control and the standard unique-fixed-point apparatus is unavailable. The literature review below substantiates both points.

Our main result is that threshold policies are optimal under all three criteria: there exists a critical inventory level at which the decision maker processes the batch and continues accumulating below it (Theorems 1, 2, and 3). Beyond optimality, we characterize the threshold exactly in each regime. Under the risk-neutral criterion, the value of every threshold policy is given by an exact, strictly unimodal scalar objective, so the optimal threshold is identified by a discrete ascent that terminates after finitely many evaluations. Under the risk-seeking criterion, the reduced objective is strictly discretely concave, and the optimal threshold is marked by an explicit marginal-cost condition: the first level at which the marginal risk-sensitive cost of accumulation reaches the marginal processing reward. Under the risk-averse criterion, we replace the unregularized entropic continuation branch by a capped robust dual formulation—a minimax stochastic game in which an adversary perturbs the transition law subject to a relative-entropy penalty and a capped likelihood ratio—and show that it admits a unique fixed point, an optimal threshold policy, and a worst-case transition law of explicit truncated-Gibbs form.

A central contribution of this paper is a unified method for establishing threshold optimality on an unbounded state space. Rather than relying on state-space truncation or backward induction, our approach exploits the skip-free upward dynamics of the inventory process and the linear structure of the one-period cost. We characterize the value of each threshold policy through forward recursions and reduce the original stopping problem to a one-dimensional optimization. A coupling argument establishes that restricting attention to threshold policies entails no loss of optimality. Together, these results provide an exact characterization of the optimal policy while avoiding artificial restrictions on the inventory level.

The three regimes also exhibit a clear structural relationship: risk aversion accelerates processing relative to the risk-neutral benchmark, whereas risk seeking delays it, and both risk-sensitive thresholds converge to an optimal threshold of the undiscounted risk-neutral problem as the risk-sensitivity parameter vanishes, with the risk-averse limit selecting the smallest risk-neutral optimal threshold when multiple optima exist (Proposition 8). The ordering further yields an exact truncation point for the numerical solution of the regularized risk-averse problem.

Our numerical study confirms the comparative statics implied by the theory, including the finding that the response of the optimal threshold to the per-item reward can reverse sign depending on the discount factor. The risk-sensitive experiments quantify the risk-seeking premium and the risk-averse discount: risk seeking shifts the optimal threshold upward by deflating the marginal cost of accumulation, whereas regularized risk aversion shifts it downward by closing the stopping gap earlier. Both thresholds converge to the risk-neutral benchmark as the risk-sensitivity parameter approaches 0, consistent with the theoretical ordering and continuity results. The experiments also characterize the worst-case abandonment distortion under the likelihood-ratio cap and illustrate the operational cost of over-batching: as the buffer grows, abandonment increasingly offsets arrivals, cycle lengths grow disproportionately, and repeated-clearing performance deteriorates.

Finally, we return to repeated clearing: in the applications above, clearing is a recurring event rather than a terminal one. Section 3 develops a repeated-clearing formulation in which each clearing resets the buffer to zero and the controller faces the same batching decision again, optimizing either the long-run average reward or the total discounted reward over infinitely many regenerative cycles. The first-passage decomposition extends with a single additional object—a time-accumulation function that prices the expected cycle length—and yields scalar reduced objectives for both repeated-clearing criteria. Threshold policies remain optimal among all stationary clearing policies. Moreover, both repeated-clearing objectives are strictly unimodal over the full threshold range: their increments admit a single sign change, characterized by a strictly decreasing marginal-rate function that prices the net reward of extending the cycle against its marginal length. The optimal threshold for repeated clearing is therefore computable exactly by a discrete ascent that terminates at the first nonpositive marginal improvement, as in the risk-neutral analysis—with no state-space truncation and no a priori bound on the search range. Furthermore, this threshold never exceeds the corresponding optimal-stopping threshold: the latter prices the erosion of value within a cycle but not the opportunity cost of the cycle length itself, and therefore systematically over-batches.

1.1 Literature Review

Batch Clearing Systems. Operationally, our model is a batch clearing system without service: the controller decides when to clear the accumulated inventory, but clearing neither occupies a server nor delays future arrivals. Stidham Jr (1974) and Whitt (1981) analyzed clearing processes in stochastic input systems, characterizing the stationary distribution of the accumulated quantity under exogenous clearing schemes. Ross (1969), Ross (1971) studied optimal clearing of Poisson processes and established the optimality of threshold policies under linear holding costs, while Kella et al. (2003) extended the analysis to clearing systems with both Brownian and compound Poisson input. These works share the feature that inventory is not lost item by item before clearing: the accumulated input is removed only at clearing epochs. The optimal stopping problems studied here, however, differ from this long-run average-cost formulation; the repeated-clearing extension of Section 3 bridges the two, adopting the long-run average and discounted criteria of the clearing literature while retaining the item-by-item abandonment that distinguishes the present model.

Batch Service and Dispatching in Queueing Systems. A related queueing literature studies batch service, where the controller repeatedly decides when to initiate service of a batch while arrivals continue during the service itself—in effect, a repeated optimal stopping problem in which each service completion renews the stopping decision. Deb and Serfozo (1973) established the optimality of threshold policies for batch-service queues, and Deb (1976) extended this analysis to settings with switching costs. Weiss (1979) developed methods for computing optimal control limits for such queues, while Xia et al. (2002) analyzed the optimal control of parallel queues with batch service. van Leeuwen and Núñez Queija (2017) studied optimal batch dispatching in a tandem of two single-server Markovian queues with batch service at the first station. Browne et al. (1992) studied gated service in infinite-server queues with Poisson arrivals and uniform service times, in which service begins for a batch whenever all jobs in the preceding batch have been completed and the queue is nonempty. The closest antecedent is Larrañaga et al. (2015), who studied optimal batching in a single-server queue with abandonment under a long-run average-cost criterion. The renewal formulation of Section 3 adopts the same long-run average criterion as Larrañaga et al. (2015) and the classical batch-service models, but differs in that there is no service in our model (no server is occupied), so the cycle length is governed by the accumulation-and-abandonment dynamics alone. Related work also considers vehicle or shuttle dispatching between two stations with transportation times (Deb 1978).

Optimal Stopping of Discrete-Time Markov Chains. The classical theory of optimal stopping for discrete-time Markov chains with time-additive cost structures (Shiryaev 2008, Peskir and Shiryaev 2006) delivers the existence of optimal stopping rules through the theory of excessive functions and Snell envelopes, and it yields control-limit (threshold) policies when the underlying dynamic program exhibits submodularity or supermodularity—monotonicity-based sufficient conditions that, as noted above, do not apply directly to our cost structure. Moreover, although Snell-envelope theory exists on general state spaces under integrability conditions, generic backward induction on a countably infinite grid is not directly implementable: without additional structure, computation uses a finite truncation whose level must be justified or controlled (Puterman 2014). We avoid this issue by exploiting the skip-free dynamics and linear cost structure of the present problem, which establish the crucial value-function decomposition that leads to a strictly unimodal reduced objective and yields the optimal threshold exactly, without truncation or backward induction.

Risk-Sensitive Optimal Stopping of Markov Chains. Risk-sensitive Markov decision problems, in which the expected additive cost is replaced by an exponential (multiplicative) criterion, equivalently an entropic criterion, are well studied (Howard and Matheson 1972, Denardo and Rothblum 1979, Borkar and Meyn 2002, Ruszczyński 2010, Pichler et al. 2022, Ren et al. 2025). Risk-sensitive optimal stopping in particular has attracted growing attention: Nagai (2007) analyzed stopping problems for multiplicative functionals, Bäuerle and Popp (2018) treated risk-sensitive stopping of continuous-time Markov chains, and Jelito et al. (2021) developed a general theory of entropic optimal stopping; a finite-horizon treatment of the associated stopping problems was developed by Palczewski and Stettner (2010). These results, however, are developed under boundedness or regularity conditions on the costs that do not cover our setting, in which both the running cost and the terminal reward grow linearly in the inventory level and are therefore unbounded on an unbounded state space. The obstacle is not merely technical: for risk-sensitive optimal stopping with an unbounded terminal cost, Jelito and Stettner (2022) showed that the associated Bellman equation may admit multiple solutions, of which only the minimal and maximal ones carry a probabilistic interpretation. In the risk-averse regime, our model circumvents this difficulty through the equivalent minimax stochastic game formulation of the entropic criterion, regularized via the Donsker–Varadhan variational formula (Donsker and Varadhan 1975, Dupuis and Ellis 2011): the stopping problem is recast as a minimax stochastic game in which an adversary perturbs the reference transition law subject to an entropy penalty or constraint (James 1992, Dai Pra et al. 1996, Petersen et al. 2000). The robust-MDP and distributionally robust literature is related but not equivalent. Classical rectangular robust MDPs typically assume finite state and action spaces or rely on bounded rewards and contraction properties (Nilim and El Ghaoui 2005, Iyengar 2005, Wiesemann et al. 2013). Subsequent general-state and approximation results exist, but they do not provide the threshold characterization sought here. In our setting, the likelihood-ratio cap is not primarily a model-uncertainty set; it is a regularization that restores uniform integrability and a uniform Foster–Lyapunov drift estimate for the regularized operator.

1.2 Organization of the Paper

Section 2 formulates the model and presents the main results: Section 2.2 treats the risk-neutral criterion, Section 2.3 the risk-seeking criterion, and Section 2.4 the regularized risk-averse criterion. Section 2.5 compares the optimal thresholds across regimes. Section 3 develops the renewal formulation for repeated clearing under the long-run average and discounted repeated-clearing criteria, and Section 4 presents the numerical study. Sections 5–7 prove Theorems 1–3, with supporting lemmas and the proofs of the repeated-clearing results deferred to the Appendix, and Section 8 concludes.

2 Model and Results

2.1 Problem Formulation

Consider an infinite-horizon, discrete-time Markovian system {Xt}t≥0\{X_{t}\}_{t\geq 0} taking values in 𝒮:=ℤ+\mathcal{S}:=\mathbb{Z}_{+}, with dynamics as follows.

State dynamics.

  1. (i)

    Arrivals. An external arrival occurs with probability q∈(0,1)q\in(0,1). Let {Dt}t≥0\{D_{t}\}_{t\geq 0} be a sequence of i.i.d. Bernoulli random variables with ℙ⁡(Dt=1)=q\mathbb{P}(D_{t}=1)=q, representing arrivals.

  2. (ii)

    Abandonment. Each of the items present independently survives the period with probability 1−p1-p, where p∈(0,1)p\in(0,1). Conditional on Xt=xX_{t}=x, the number of departures in period tt is At​(x)∼Binomial⁡(x,p)A_{t}(x)\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(x,p). Abandonment occurs independently of arrivals.

Conditional on continuation, the state transition dynamics are

Xt+1=Xt−At(Xt)+Dt,t=0,1,2,….X_{t+1}=X_{t}-A_{t}(X_{t})+D_{t},\qquad t=0,1,2,\dots. (1)

XtX_{t} is the inventory level at the beginning of period tt. We write 𝒫⁡(x,⋅)\mathcal{P}(x,\cdot) for the one-step transition kernel induced by (1). Because 0<p,q<10<p,q<1, this kernel assigns positive probability to every state in {0,1,…,x+1}\{0,1,\dots,x+1\} and zero probability elsewhere. Throughout, AxA_{x} denotes a generic Binomial⁡(x,p)\operatorname{Binomial}(x,p) random variable and DD a generic Bernoulli⁡(q)\operatorname{Bernoulli}(q) random variable, independent of AxA_{x}.

Action space and admissible policies. At the beginning of each period tt, the decision maker chooses an action at∈𝒜={stop,continue}a_{t}\in\mathcal{A}=\{\textsc{stop},\textsc{continue}\}. Choosing stop terminates the process and triggers a batch operation; choosing continue allows the system to evolve for another period. A stationary deterministic Markov policy is a mapping π:𝒮→𝒜\pi:\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{A}. Of particular interest is the class of stationary threshold policies indexed by θ∈ℤ+\theta\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}:

πθ​(x)={continue,x<θ,stop,x≥θ.\pi_{\theta}(x)=\begin{cases}\textsc{continue},&x<\theta,\\ \textsc{stop},&x\geq\theta.\end{cases} (2)

Under πθ\pi_{\theta}, the associated stopping time is the first-entrance time into {θ,θ+1,…}\{\theta,\theta+1,\dots\}, namely τθ:=inf{t≥0:Xt≥θ}\tau_{\theta}:=\inf\{t\geq 0:X_{t}\geq\theta\}. Restricting attention to this class entails no loss of optimality under any criterion analyzed below: Propositions 2 and 6 establish this for the risk-neutral and risk-seeking problems, respectively, and Theorem 3(ii) does so for the regularized risk-averse problem.

Economic primitives. Let δ∈(0,1]\delta\in(0,1] denote the per-period discount factor. The cost and reward structure consists of a fixed stopping cost α>0\alpha>0 incurred upon stopping; a reward coefficient β>0\beta>0 earned per item processed in the batch; a per-period holding cost c>0c>0 per item in the buffer; and an abandonment penalty γ>0\gamma>0 per item departing before processing. Holding costs are charged on beginning-of-period inventory, whereas abandonments are realized at the end of the period. The abandonment penalty is therefore discounted by one additional factor of δ\delta relative to the holding cost in (3). We write 𝒞:=c+δ​γ​p>0\mathcal{C}:=c+\delta\gamma p>0 for the effective expected one-stage cost rate and S⁡(x):=β​x−αS(x):=\beta x-\alpha for the stopping (terminal) reward.

The optimization problems. For each x∈𝒮x\in\mathcal{S}, we write ℙx\mathbb{P}_{x} for the law of the chain (1) started at X0=xX_{0}=x and 𝔼x\mathbb{E}_{x} for the associated expectation. For a stopping time τ\tau, define the total discounted reward along the trajectory by

ℛδ​(τ):=δτ​(β​Xτ−α)−∑t=0τ−1δt​(c​Xt+δ​γ​At​(Xt)).\mathcal{R}_{\delta}(\tau):=\delta^{\tau}(\beta X_{\tau}-\alpha)-\sum_{t=0}^{\tau-1}\delta^{t}\bigl(cX_{t}+\delta\gamma A_{t}(X_{t})\bigr). (3)

The risk-neutral and entropic risk-sensitive criteria from the initial state x∈𝒮x\in\mathcal{S} are, respectively,

Jr​n​(x,τ):=𝔼x​[ℛδ​(τ)],J_{rn}(x,\tau):=\mathbb{E}_{x}\!\left[\mathcal{R}_{\delta}(\tau)\right], (4)
Jr​(x,τ):=1η​log⁡𝔼x​[eη​ℛδ​(τ)],η∈ℝ∖{0}.J_{r}(x,\tau):=\frac{1}{\eta}\log\mathbb{E}_{x}\!\left[e^{\eta\mathcal{R}_{\delta}(\tau)}\right],\qquad\eta\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}. (5)

Vr​n​(x):=supτ∈𝔗Jr​n​(x,τ),x∈𝒮,V_{rn}(x):=\sup_{\tau\in\mathfrak{T}}J_{rn}(x,\tau),\quad x\in\mathcal{S}, (6)

2.1.1 The Skip-Free Property

The chain {Xt}t≥0\{X_{t}\}_{t\geq 0} is skip-free to the right, so every upward first passage traverses all intermediate levels.

Lemma 1.

The DTMC {Xt}\{X_{t}\} governed by (1) is skip-free to the right: for every x∈𝒮x\in\mathcal{S} and every t≥0t\geq 0,

ℙ⁡(Xt+1≤x+1∣Xt=x)=1,\mathbb{P}(X_{t+1}\leq x+1\mid X_{t}=x)=1,
ℙ⁡(Xt+1=x+1∣Xt=x)=(1−p)x​q>0.\mathbb{P}(X_{t+1}=x+1\mid X_{t}=x)=(1-p)^{x}q>0.

Moreover, every state y∈{0,1,…,x+1}y\in\{0,1,\dots,x+1\} is reachable from xx in one step.

2.2.2 Increment Bound and Threshold Structure

The reduction to threshold policies rests on a uniform bound on the increments of the value function.

Lemma 2 (Increments of the value function).

For all x∈𝒮x\in\mathcal{S}, Vr​n​(x+1)−Vr​n​(x)≤βV_{rn}(x+1)-V_{rn}(x)\leq\beta.

Proposition 2 (Threshold structure of optimal policies).

The optimal stopping region 𝒮∗:={x∈𝒮:Vr​n​(x)=β​x−α}\mathcal{S}^{*}:=\{x\in\mathcal{S}:V_{rn}(x)=\beta x-\alpha\} is up-closed: x∈𝒮∗x\in\mathcal{S}^{*} implies x+1∈𝒮∗x+1\in\mathcal{S}^{*}. Consequently, whenever the supremum in (6) is attained by the first-entrance rule into 𝒮∗\mathcal{S}^{*}, that rule is the stationary threshold policy πθ∗\pi_{\theta^{*}} with θ∗=min⁡𝒮∗\theta^{*}=\min\mathcal{S}^{*}.

Proposition 2 reduces problem (6) to a one-dimensional search over the integer threshold θ\theta. The remainder of this section makes the search efficient: Section 2.2.3 derives a reduced objective that is computable by a forward recursion, and Section 2.2.4 shows that this objective is strictly unimodal with an attained maximizer, so the search terminates at the first local maximizer.

2.2.3 Value-Function Decomposition

Fix a threshold θ∈ℤ+\theta\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}. Because the one-stage cost is linear in the state and, by Lemma 1, the first passage to θ\theta traverses every intermediate level, the value function under πθ\pi_{\theta} decomposes additively along the trajectory. The decomposition is anchored at state 00 and captured by two auxiliary sequences. Write

ωx:=1−δ​(1−p)x​(1−q),x≥0.\omega_{x}:=1-\delta(1-p)^{x}(1-q),\qquad x\geq 0.

Define f:𝒮→ℝf:\mathcal{S}\to\mathbb{R}, the cost-accumulation function, by f⁡(0)=0f(0)=0 and the forward recurrence

f⁡(x+1)=𝒞​x+ωx​f​(x)−δ​F​(x)δ​(1−p)x​q,x≥0,f(x+1)=\frac{\mathcal{C}x+\omega_{x}f(x)-\delta F(x)}{\delta(1-p)^{x}q},\quad x\geq 0, (10)

where

F⁡(x)=𝔼Ax,D​[𝟏Ax≥1⋅f⁡(X^x)]F(x)=\mathbb{E}_{A_{x},D}\!\bigl[\mathbf{1}_{A_{x}\geq 1}\cdot f(\hat{X}_{x})\bigr] (11)

aggregates the contribution of periods with strictly positive attrition. Define g:𝒮→ℝg:\mathcal{S}\to\mathbb{R}, the discount-accumulation function, by g⁡(0)=1g(0)=1 and

g⁡(x+1)=ωx​g​(x)−δ​G​(x)δ​(1−p)x​q,x≥0,g(x+1)=\frac{\omega_{x}g(x)-\delta G(x)}{\delta(1-p)^{x}q},\quad x\geq 0, (12)

where

G⁡(x)=𝔼Ax,D​[𝟏Ax≥1⋅g⁡(X^x)].G(x)=\mathbb{E}_{A_{x},D}\!\bigl[\mathbf{1}_{A_{x}\geq 1}\cdot g(\hat{X}_{x})\bigr]. (13)

Both are proper forward recursions: on {Ax≥1}\{A_{x}\geq 1\} one has X^x≤x\hat{X}_{x}\leq x, so F⁡(x)F(x) and G⁡(x)G(x) depend only on values of ff and gg at states 0,…,x0,\dots,x.

Remark 1 (Fixed-point form of the recurrences).

The recurrences (10) and (12) are equivalent to

f⁡(x)=−𝒞​x+δ​𝔼​[f⁡(X^x)],f(x)=-\mathcal{C}x+\delta\,\mathbb{E}[f(\hat{X}_{x})], (14)
g⁡(x)=δ​𝔼​[g⁡(X^x)].g(x)=\delta\,\mathbb{E}[g(\hat{X}_{x})]. (15)

Indeed, conditioning on AxA_{x} and solving for f⁡(x+1)f(x+1) and g⁡(x+1)g(x+1) gives the original recurrences. Binomial thinning also implies that, for every u:ℤ+→ℝu:\mathbb{Z}_{+}\to\mathbb{R} and k≥1k\geq 1,

Δk​𝔼​[u⁡(Yx)]=(1−p)k​𝔼​[Δk​u​(Yx)],\Delta^{k}\,\mathbb{E}[u(Y_{x})]=(1-p)^{k}\,\mathbb{E}[\Delta^{k}u(Y_{x})], (16)

where Δ​u​(x):=u⁡(x+1)−u⁡(x)\Delta u(x):=u(x+1)-u(x) is the forward-difference operator, Δk\Delta^{k} its kk-th iterate, and Yx:=x−Ax∼Binomial⁡(x,1−p)Y_{x}:=x-A_{x}\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(x,1-p).

Proposition 3.

Fix θ∈ℤ+\theta\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}, let Vr​n,πθ​(x):=Jr​n​(x,τθ)V_{rn,\pi_{\theta}}(x):=J_{rn}(x,\tau_{\theta}) denote the value function under πθ\pi_{\theta} started from xx, and write vr​n​(θ):=Vr​n,πθ​(0)v_{rn}(\theta):=V_{rn,\pi_{\theta}}(0) for the reduced objective.

  1. (i)

    (Affine decomposition) For every initial state x∈𝒮x\in\mathcal{S} and every threshold θ≥x\theta\geq x,

    Vr​n,πθ​(x)=g⁡(x)​vr​n​(θ)+f⁡(x),V_{rn,\pi_{\theta}}(x)=g(x)\,v_{rn}(\theta)+f(x), (17)

    while over thresholds θ≤x\theta\leq x the policy stops immediately and Vr​n,πθ​(x)=β​x−αV_{rn,\pi_{\theta}}(x)=\beta x-\alpha is independent of θ\theta. For fixed xx, the right-hand side of (17) is a strictly increasing affine transformation of the reduced objective, so every maximizer θ∗≥x\theta^{*}\geq x of vr​nv_{rn} also maximizes θ↦Vr​n,πθ​(x)\theta\mapsto V_{rn,\pi_{\theta}}(x) over all θ∈ℤ+\theta\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}.

  2. (ii)

    (Discounted reduced objective) For δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), g⁡(x)≥1g(x)\geq 1 and

    vr​n​(θ)=β​θ−α−f⁡(θ)g⁡(θ).v_{rn}(\theta)\;=\;\frac{\beta\theta-\alpha-f(\theta)}{g(\theta)}. (18)
  3. (iii)

    (Undiscounted reduced objective) For δ=1\delta=1, g⁡(x)≡1g(x)\equiv 1 and

    vr​n​(θ)=β​θ−α−f⁡(θ).v_{rn}(\theta)\;=\;\beta\theta-\alpha-f(\theta). (19)

Maximizing the reduced objective anchored at the reference state 00 therefore yields, in a single one-dimensional search, a threshold policy that is optimal among threshold policies from every initial state simultaneously.

Remark 2 (Operational interpretations of ff and gg).

Let

Cθ:=𝔼0​[∑t=0Tθ−1δt​(c​Xt+δ​γ​At​(Xt))]C_{\theta}:=\mathbb{E}_{0}\!\left[\sum_{t=0}^{T_{\theta}-1}\delta^{t}\bigl(cX_{t}+\delta\gamma A_{t}(X_{t})\bigr)\right]

denote the expected present value of the holding and abandonment costs accrued during the first passage from the reference state 00 to θ\theta. Directly from (3), using XTθ=θX_{T_{\theta}}=\theta,

Vr​n,πθ​(0)=(β​θ−α)​𝔼0​[δTθ]−Cθ.V_{rn,\pi_{\theta}}(0)=(\beta\theta-\alpha)\,\mathbb{E}_{0}\!\left[\delta^{T_{\theta}}\right]-C_{\theta}.

Because ff and gg do not depend on α\alpha or β\beta, matching the coefficient of β​θ−α\beta\theta-\alpha and the constant term with those in (18) identifies

𝔼0​[δTθ]=1g⁡(θ),Cθ=f⁡(θ)g⁡(θ).\mathbb{E}_{0}\!\left[\delta^{T_{\theta}}\right]=\frac{1}{g(\theta)},\qquad C_{\theta}=\frac{f(\theta)}{g(\theta)}.

Thus g⁡(θ)g(\theta) is the reciprocal of the expected discount factor over the first passage, and f⁡(θ)f(\theta) is the expected present value of the first-passage costs expressed in units of 𝔼0​[δTθ]\mathbb{E}_{0}[\delta^{T_{\theta}}]. Only when δ=1\delta=1 do g⁡(θ)g(\theta) and f⁡(θ)f(\theta) coincide with 𝔼0​[δTθ]\mathbb{E}_{0}[\delta^{T_{\theta}}] and CθC_{\theta} themselves.

By Proposition 2 and Proposition 3(i), the search for an optimal policy from any initial state reduces to maximizing the reduced objective vr​nv_{rn}, whose evaluation requires only the forward iterates of (10)–(12); the remainder of this section analyzes vr​nv_{rn} alone.

2.2.4 The Optimal Threshold

To rule out the degenerate regime in which no batch is ever profitable, we impose a standing assumption.

Assumption 1 (Profitability).

There exists at least one θ∈ℤ+\theta\in\mathbb{Z}_{+} such that

Nr​n​(θ):=β​θ−α−f⁡(θ)> 0.N_{rn}(\theta)\;:=\;\beta\theta-\alpha-f(\theta)\;>\;0. (20)

Write Θ+:={θ∈ℤ+:Nr​n​(θ)>0}\Theta_{+}:=\{\theta\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}:N_{rn}(\theta)>0\} for the positive domain of the numerator and θ¯:=max⁡Θ+\overline{\theta}:=\max\Theta_{+} for its largest element whenever Θ+\Theta_{+} is finite; Assumption 1 is imposed throughout the remainder of this subsection.

Theorem 1 (Optimal risk-neutral policy).

Suppose that Assumption 1 holds.

  1. (i)

    (Strict unimodality) On its positive domain Θ+\Theta_{+}, the reduced objective is strictly unimodal: there exists θu∈Θ+\theta^{u}\in\Theta_{+} such that Δ​vr​n​(θ)>0\Delta v_{rn}(\theta)>0 for θ<θu\theta<\theta^{u}, Δ​vr​n​(θu)≤0\Delta v_{rn}(\theta^{u})\leq 0, and Δ​vr​n​(θ)<0\Delta v_{rn}(\theta)<0 for θu<θ≤θ¯\theta^{u}<\theta\leq\overline{\theta}.

  2. (ii)

    (Tail behavior) For δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), define

    C∞:=δ​q​𝒞(1−δ)​(1−δ⁡(1−p)).C_{\infty}:=\frac{\delta q\,\mathcal{C}}{(1-\delta)\bigl(1-\delta(1-p)\bigr)}. (21)

    Then

    limθ→∞vr​n​(θ)={−C∞,if ​δ<1,−∞,if ​δ=1.\lim_{\theta\to\infty}v_{rn}(\theta)=\begin{cases}-C_{\infty},&\text{if }\delta<1,\\[6.0pt] -\infty,&\text{if }\delta=1.\end{cases} (22)
  3. (iii)

    (Optimal threshold) The index

    θr​n∗=min⁡{θ∈ℤ+:Δ​vr​n​(θ)≤0}\theta^{*}_{rn}=\min\bigl\{\theta\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}:\Delta v_{rn}(\theta)\leq 0\bigr\} (23)

    is well defined and finite, coincides with θu\theta^{u}, and is the smallest optimal threshold: at most two thresholds are optimal, and they differ by one. The threshold policy πθr​n∗\pi_{\theta^{*}_{rn}} is optimal among all admissible policies from every initial state: its value function Vr​n,πθr​n∗V_{rn,\pi_{\theta^{*}_{rn}}} solves the Bellman equation (9) and coincides with Vr​nV_{rn}, and the optimal stopping region is 𝒮∗={θr​n∗,θr​n∗+1,…}\mathcal{S}^{*}=\{\theta^{*}_{rn},\theta^{*}_{rn}+1,\dots\}. Moreover,

    Vr​n​(0)=vr​n​(θr​n∗)=maxθ∈ℤ+⁡vr​n​(θ).V_{rn}(0)\;=\;v_{rn}(\theta^{*}_{rn})\;=\;\max_{\theta\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}}v_{rn}(\theta). (24)

The proof is given in Section 5. Theorem 1 justifies a discrete ascent—evaluate vr​n​(0),vr​n​(1),…v_{rn}(0),v_{rn}(1),\dots and stop at the first index with Δ​vr​n​(θ)≤0\Delta v_{rn}(\theta)\leq 0—that terminates after finitely many evaluations at the smallest optimal threshold.

Remark 3 (The degenerate case).

If (20) fails, then no batch recoups the fixed cost of processing it: Nr​n​(θ)≤0N_{rn}(\theta)\leq 0 for every θ\theta, the positive domain Θ+\Theta_{+} is empty, and the unimodality statement of Theorem 1(i) is vacuous. In this regime, operating the system is never profitable, and the interesting question concerns whether, rather than when, to clear the buffer. We exclude it throughout: the comparison and regularization results of Sections 2.4 and 2.5 that involve θr​n∗\theta^{*}_{rn}—in particular the truncation certificate Xmax=θr​n∗X_{\max}=\theta^{*}_{rn} of Remark 8—are all stated under Assumption 1.

2.3 Risk-Seeking Optimal Batching

We now turn to the entropic criterion (5).

Assumption 2.

The risk-sensitive analysis is restricted to the undiscounted case δ=1\delta=1.

Remark 4.

Under discounting, stationary multiplicative separability is lost: for δ<1\delta<1, the certainty equivalent still satisfies a Bellman recursion, but the risk parameter is discounted together with the reward, η↦η​δ\eta\mapsto\eta\delta, so the value function is defined on the augmented state (x,λ)(x,\lambda) and the optimal stopping region is a boundary in the (x,λ)(x,\lambda)-plane rather than a fixed threshold (Chung and Sobel 1987). The decomposition of Proposition 5 requires the undiscounted setting, in which the same η\eta appears at every step; the discounted case can be solved numerically (Section A).

2.3.1 Bellman Equation

Throughout the risk-seeking analysis (Sections 2.3.1–2.3.3), we write Vr​s:=VrV_{rs}:=V_{r} for the optimal entropic value (7) with η>0\eta>0. Let

Qr​(x):=−c​x+1η​log⁡𝔼⁡[eη⁡(Vr​(X^x)−γ​Ax)]Q_{r}(x):=-cx+\frac{1}{\eta}\log\mathbb{E}\!\left[e^{\eta(V_{r}(\hat{X}_{x})-\gamma A_{x})}\right] (25)

denote the continuation branch. By multiplicative separability, the associated value function satisfies the Bellman equation

Vr​(x)=max⁡{S⁡(x),Qr​(x)}.V_{r}(x)=\max\!\left\{S(x),\,Q_{r}(x)\right\}. (26)

Well-posedness of (26) for η>0\eta>0 rests on a pathwise envelope for the undiscounted reward, which exists because holding costs accumulate superlinearly along any excursion while the terminal reward grows only linearly.

Proposition 4 (Well-posedness of the risk-seeking Bellman equation).

Let η>0\eta>0 and define

U¯​(x):=(β+c/2)22​c−α+c2​x​(x−1),x∈ℤ+.\bar{U}(x):=\frac{(\beta+c/2)^{2}}{2c}-\alpha+\frac{c}{2}\,x(x-1),\qquad x\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}.
  1. (i)

    (Pathwise envelope) For every xx and every almost surely finite stopping time τ\tau,

    ℛ1​(τ)≤U¯​(x)ℙx​-almost surely.\mathcal{R}_{1}(\tau)\leq\bar{U}(x)\qquad\mathbb{P}_{x}\text{-almost surely}.

    Consequently, β​x−α≤Vr​s​(x)≤U¯​(x)\beta x-\alpha\leq V_{rs}(x)\leq\bar{U}(x) for all xx. Moreover, along the chain under any policy, for every t≥0t\geq 0, ℙx\mathbb{P}_{x}-almost surely,

    Vr​s​(Xt)−∑s=0t−1(c​Xs+γ​As​(Xs))≤U¯​(x).V_{rs}(X_{t})-\sum_{s=0}^{t-1}\bigl(cX_{s}+\gamma A_{s}(X_{s})\bigr)\leq\bar{U}(x).
  2. (ii)

    (Dynamic programming) Vr​sV_{rs} satisfies the Bellman equation (26), and all expectations therein are finite.

  3. (iii)

    (Minimality and value iteration) Let 𝒯r​s\mathcal{T}_{rs} denote the Bellman operator defined by the right-hand side of (26). The iterates u0​(x)=β​x−αu_{0}(x)=\beta x-\alpha and un+1=𝒯r​s​unu_{n+1}=\mathcal{T}_{rs}u_{n} increase pointwise to Vr​sV_{rs}. Moreover, Vr​sV_{rs} is the minimal solution of (26) dominating the stopping reward: every solution V^\widehat{V} with V^​(x)≥β​x−α\widehat{V}(x)\geq\beta x-\alpha for all xx satisfies V^≥Vr​s\widehat{V}\geq V_{rs}.

Proofs of the propositions and lemmas in Sections 2.3.1, 2.3.2, and 2.3.3 are deferred to Section C.

2.3.2 Risk-Seeking Value-Function Decomposition

We extend the decomposition method of Section 2.2.3 to the risk-seeking case (η>0\eta>0). Write

ωr​s​(x):=eη​c​x−(1−p)x​(1−q),x≥0.\omega_{rs}(x):=e^{\eta cx}-(1-p)^{x}(1-q),\qquad x\geq 0.

Define fr​s:ℤ+→ℝf_{rs}:\mathbb{Z}_{+}\to\mathbb{R}, the risk-sensitive cost-accumulation function, by fr​s​(0)=0f_{rs}(0)=0 and for x≥0x\geq 0

fr​s​(x+1)=1η​log⁡(eη​fr​s​(x)​ωr​s​(x)−Fr​s​(x)(1−p)x​q),f_{rs}(x+1)=\frac{1}{\eta}\log\!\left(\frac{e^{\eta f_{rs}(x)}\omega_{rs}(x)-F_{rs}(x)}{(1-p)^{x}q}\right), (27)

where the risk-adjusted attrition operator Fr​s:ℤ+→ℝF_{rs}:\mathbb{Z}_{+}\to\mathbb{R} is

Fr​s​(x)=𝔼Ax,D​[𝟏Ax≥1⋅eη⁡(fr​s​(X^x)−γ​Ax)].F_{rs}(x)=\mathbb{E}_{A_{x},D}\!\left[\mathbf{1}_{A_{x}\geq 1}\cdot e^{\eta(f_{rs}(\hat{X}_{x})-\gamma A_{x})}\right]. (28)

The recurrence (27) is the risk-sensitive analogue of (10): the factor eη​c​xe^{\eta cx} captures the certain holding cost, while Fr​s​(x)F_{rs}(x) aggregates the uncertain attrition-adjusted continuation. It is a proper forward recursion by the same argument as in Section 2.2.3, and Proposition 12(i) shows that the argument of the logarithm is strictly positive at every state, so the recursion is well posed.

Proposition 5 (Risk-seeking value decomposition).

Fix θ∈ℤ+\theta\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}, let Vr​s,πθ​(x):=Jr​(x,τθ)V_{rs,\pi_{\theta}}(x):=J_{r}(x,\tau_{\theta}) denote the risk-seeking value function under πθ\pi_{\theta} started from xx, and write vr​s​(θ):=Vr​s,πθ​(0)v_{rs}(\theta):=V_{rs,\pi_{\theta}}(0) for the risk-seeking reduced objective.

  1. (i)

    (Additive decomposition) For every initial state x∈𝒮x\in\mathcal{S} and every threshold θ>x\theta>x,

    Vr​s,πθ​(x)=fr​s​(x)+vr​s​(θ),V_{rs,\pi_{\theta}}(x)=f_{rs}(x)+v_{rs}(\theta), (29)

    while over thresholds θ≤x\theta\leq x, the policy stops immediately and Vr​s,πθ​(x)=β​x−αV_{rs,\pi_{\theta}}(x)=\beta x-\alpha is independent of θ\theta. For fixed xx, the right-hand side of (29) differs from the reduced objective by the θ\theta-independent constant fr​s​(x)f_{rs}(x), so every maximizer θ∗≥x\theta^{*}\geq x of vr​sv_{rs} also maximizes θ↦Vr​s,πθ​(x)\theta\mapsto V_{rs,\pi_{\theta}}(x) over all θ∈ℤ+\theta\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}.

  2. (ii)

    (Reduced objective) The function fr​sf_{rs} does not depend on θ\theta, and

    vr​s​(θ)=β​θ−α−fr​s​(θ).v_{rs}(\theta)=\beta\theta-\alpha-f_{rs}(\theta). (30)
Remark 5 (Certainty-equivalent interpretation).

Write Cx→yC_{x\to y} for the cost accumulated by the always-continue policy from state xx until the first passage to y>xy>x. By (68), fr​s​(x)f_{rs}(x) is the entropic certainty equivalent of the first-passage cost C0→xC_{0\to x}, and the marginal cost Δ​fr​s​(x)\Delta f_{rs}(x) is that of a single one-level excursion Cx→x+1C_{x\to x+1} (Proposition 13). For η>0\eta>0, risk seeking deflates marginal costs relative to the undiscounted risk-neutral benchmark, Δ​fr​s≤Δ​f\Delta f_{rs}\leq\Delta f, and consequently pushes the optimal threshold upward (Proposition 13(ii)–(iii)).

2.3.3 Optimal Threshold Under the Risk-Seeking Criterion

The increment bound of Lemma 2 extends to the entropic criterion, reducing the search for an optimal policy to the threshold family; the reduced objective (30) then yields the optimal threshold exactly. The increment Δ​fr​s​(x)\Delta f_{rs}(x) is the marginal risk-sensitive cost of increasing the state from xx to x+1x+1.

Lemma 3 (Increment bound).

For all x≥0x\geq 0, Vr​s​(x+1)−Vr​s​(x)≤βV_{rs}(x+1)-V_{rs}(x)\leq\beta.

Proposition 6 (Threshold policies suffice).

The stopping region {x≥0:Vr​s​(x)=β​x−α}\{x\geq 0:V_{rs}(x)=\beta x-\alpha\} is nonempty and up-closed; writing θr​s∗\theta^{*}_{rs} for its smallest element, the threshold policy πθr​s∗\pi_{\theta^{*}_{rs}} is optimal among all admissible policies. In particular, Vr​s​(0)=maxθ≥0⁡vr​s​(θ)V_{rs}(0)=\max_{\theta\geq 0}v_{rs}(\theta).

Theorem 2 (Optimal risk-seeking policy).

Let η>0\eta>0.

  1. (i)

    The reduced objective is strictly discretely concave: Δ2​vr​s​(θ)≤−c\Delta^{2}v_{rs}(\theta)\leq-c for all θ≥0\theta\geq 0.

  2. (ii)

    The smallest optimal threshold is

    θr​s∗=min⁡{θ∈ℤ+:Δ​fr​s​(θ)≥β},\theta^{*}_{rs}=\min\bigl\{\theta\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}:\Delta f_{rs}(\theta)\geq\beta\bigr\}, (31)

    and it satisfies 1≤θr​s∗≤⌈β/c⌉1\leq\theta^{*}_{rs}\leq\lceil\beta/c\rceil.

  3. (iii)

    The optimal threshold is unique unless Δ​fr​s​(θr​s∗)=β\Delta f_{rs}(\theta^{*}_{rs})=\beta, in which case exactly the two adjacent thresholds θr​s∗\theta^{*}_{rs} and θr​s∗+1\theta^{*}_{rs}+1 are optimal. Moreover, Vr​s​(0)=vr​s​(θr​s∗)=maxθ≥0⁡vr​s​(θ)V_{rs}(0)=v_{rs}(\theta^{*}_{rs})=\max_{\theta\geq 0}v_{rs}(\theta), and πθr​s∗\pi_{\theta^{*}_{rs}} is optimal among all admissible policies.

Equivalently, θr​s∗\theta^{*}_{rs} is the smallest state at which the marginal risk-sensitive cost of increasing the state reaches the marginal processing reward.

2.4 Risk-Averse Optimal Threshold: Robust Dual Formulation

For η<0\eta<0, the unregularized entropic value remains finite, but the standard bounded-cost/contractive fixed-point apparatus does not apply on the unbounded space, and the continuation branch has no uniform lower control; indeed, Lemma 4 shows that it can diverge downward under strong risk aversion. We therefore introduce a capped KL-robust dual as a tractable regularization: it upper-bounds the entropic problem and restores tractability, admits a unique fixed point in the natural linear-growth class, preserves threshold optimality, and yields an explicit truncated-Gibbs worst-case law. Throughout this section, Assumptions 2 and 1 are in force; in particular, δ=1\delta=1.

Lemma 4 (Downward divergence of the unregularized risk-averse continuation branch).

Let η<0\eta<0. Define

Λη:=eη​β​(1−p+p​e−η⁡(β+γ)).\Lambda_{\eta}:=e^{\eta\beta}\Bigl(1-p+pe^{-\eta(\beta+\gamma)}\Bigr).

For each K∈ℝK\in\mathbb{R}, define the reward class

ℒK:={u:ℤ+→ℝ:βx−α≤u(x)≤βx+Kfor every x∈ℤ+},\mathscr{L}_{K}:=\left\{u:\mathbb{Z}_{+}\to\mathbb{R}:\beta x-\alpha\leq u(x)\leq\beta x+K\quad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}\right\},

and write the unregularized risk-averse continuation branch as

Q~r​a​(u)​(x):=−c​x+1η​log⁡𝔼⁡[eη⁡{u⁡(X^x)−γ​Ax}],X^x=x−Ax+D.\widetilde{Q}_{ra}(u)(x):=-cx+\frac{1}{\eta}\log\mathbb{E}\!\left[e^{\eta\{u(\hat{X}_{x})-\gamma A_{x}\}}\right],\qquad\hat{X}_{x}=x-A_{x}+D.

If Λη>1\Lambda_{\eta}>1, then, uniformly over u∈ℒKu\in\mathscr{L}_{K},

Q~r​a​(u)​(x)≤−(c−log⁡Ληη)​x+K+log⁡(1−q+q​eη​β)η⟶−∞(x→∞).\widetilde{Q}_{ra}(u)(x)\leq-\left(c-\frac{\log\Lambda_{\eta}}{\eta}\right)x+K+\frac{\log(1-q+qe^{\eta\beta})}{\eta}\longrightarrow-\infty\qquad(x\to\infty).

Moreover, Λη>1\Lambda_{\eta}>1 for all sufficiently large |η||\eta|.

Dual representation via the Donsker–Varadhan variational principle (Dupuis and Ellis 2011). For any bounded random variable ZZ, probability measure ℙ\mathbb{P}, and η<0\eta<0,

1ηlog𝔼ℙ[eη​Z]=infℚ≪ℙ{𝔼ℚ[Z]−1ηDKL(ℚ∥ℙ)},\frac{1}{\eta}\log\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}}\!\left[e^{\eta Z}\right]=\inf_{\mathbb{Q}\ll\mathbb{P}}\left\{\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}[Z]-\frac{1}{\eta}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathbb{Q}\,\|\,\mathbb{P})\right\}, (32)

where DKL(ℚ∥ℙ)=𝔼ℚ[log(dℚ/dℙ)]D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathbb{Q}\,\|\,\mathbb{P})=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}[\log(d\mathbb{Q}/d\mathbb{P})] is the Kullback–Leibler divergence (relative entropy) and the infimum is attained by the Gibbs measure d​ℚ∗/d​ℙ∝eη​Zd\mathbb{Q}^{*}/d\mathbb{P}\propto e^{\eta Z}.

Applying (32) to the continuation branch gives the uncapped dual continuation branch

Q~r​a(x)=−cx+infℚx∈𝒫(⋅∣x){𝔼ℚx[Vr(X^x)−γAx]−1ηDKL(ℚx∥ℙx)}.\displaystyle\widetilde{Q}_{ra}(x)=-cx+\inf_{\mathbb{Q}_{x}\in\mathcal{P}(\cdot\mid x)}\Bigl\{\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}_{x}}[V_{r}(\hat{X}_{x})-\gamma A_{x}]-\frac{1}{\eta}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathbb{Q}_{x}\,\|\,\mathbb{P}_{x})\Bigr\}. (33)

Hence

Vr​(x)=max⁡{S⁡(x),Q~r​a​(x)},V_{r}(x)=\max\!\left\{S(x),\,\widetilde{Q}_{ra}(x)\right\}, (34)

where ℙx\mathbb{P}_{x} is the nominal one-step law of the pair (Ax,D)(A_{x},D), or equivalently of X^x\hat{X}_{x}—throughout the risk-averse analysis the symbol ℙx\mathbb{P}_{x} denotes this one-step kernel, a slight overload of the path-law notation of Section 2.1—and 𝒫(⋅∣x)\mathcal{P}(\cdot\mid x) is the set of probability measures absolutely continuous with respect to ℙx\mathbb{P}_{x}. Equation (34) is the Bellman equation of a stochastic game: the decision maker chooses a stopping time, and an adversary (Nature) chooses at each state a perturbed transition kernel ℚx\mathbb{Q}_{x} that distorts the abandonment and arrival distributions so as to minimize the decision maker’s payoff, with each deviation from the nominal model penalized by the positive term −(1/η)DKL(ℚx∥ℙx)-(1/\eta)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathbb{Q}_{x}\,\|\,\mathbb{P}_{x}).

Remark 6.

The dual representation exposes the structural difference between the risk regimes. For η>0\eta>0, the infimum in (32) becomes a supremum, and the adversary cooperates with the decision maker, seeking scenarios with high reward. For η<0\eta<0, the adversary is antagonistic, seeking scenarios with high cost, but is penalized for deviating excessively from the nominal model.

Regularization via uncertainty sets. The uncapped dual formulation (34) is finite at each state, but it does not provide the uniform control needed on the unbounded state space: with the adversary constrained only by the KL penalty, distorted one-step payoffs need not satisfy a uniform integrability or drift estimate across all xx, and the associated fixed-point problem is outside the standard contraction framework. We therefore cap the likelihood ratio of the adversary’s distortion. For κ>1\kappa>1, define

𝒬κ​(x)={ℚx≪ℙx:0≤d​ℚxd​ℙx≤κ},\mathcal{Q}_{\kappa}(x)=\left\{\mathbb{Q}_{x}\ll\mathbb{P}_{x}:0\leq\frac{d\mathbb{Q}_{x}}{d\mathbb{P}_{x}}\leq\kappa\right\}, (35)

where ℙx=ℙx(A)⊗ℙx(D)\mathbb{P}_{x}=\mathbb{P}_{x}^{(A)}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{x}^{(D)} is the nominal joint distribution of the abandonment count Ax∼Binomial⁡(x,p)A_{x}\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(x,p) and the arrival D∼Bernoulli⁡(q)D\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(q). The cap serves two purposes: it keeps every distorted one-step cost uniformly integrable, and it yields the uniform Foster–Lyapunov drift estimate behind the well-posedness argument (Lemma 11). In addition, the KL penalty forces the worst-case measure to have full support (Lemma 13)—the proof exploits the boundary singularity of m​log⁡mm\log m at m=0m=0, not the cap—and this full-support property drives the uniqueness and verification arguments (Lemma 15 and Proposition 16).

Remark 7.

The nominal kernel is the product law ℙx=ℙx(A)⊗ℙx(D)\mathbb{P}_{x}=\mathbb{P}_{x}^{(A)}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{x}^{(D)} on the finite support 𝒳x={0,1,…,x}×{0,1}\mathcal{X}_{x}=\{0,1,\dots,x\}\times\{0,1\}. Because 0<p,q<10<p,q<1, every atom carries positive nominal probability, so the absolute-continuity requirement ℚx≪ℙx\mathbb{Q}_{x}\ll\mathbb{P}_{x} imposes no restriction: ℚx\mathbb{Q}_{x} may be any probability vector on the 2​(x+1)2(x+1) atoms. Two consequences are worth noting. First, ℚx\mathbb{Q}_{x} need not be a product measure: the adversary may couple abandonment and arrivals, for instance by concentrating mass on atoms where heavy abandonment coincides with an arrival, inflating the abandonment penalty and the subsequent holding load simultaneously. Second, parametric perturbations Binomial⁡(x,p′)⊗Bernoulli⁡(q′)\operatorname{Binomial}(x,p^{\prime})\otimes\operatorname{Bernoulli}(q^{\prime}) with (p′,q′)≠(p,q)(p^{\prime},q^{\prime})\neq(p,q) form only a small subfamily of 𝒫(⋅∣x)\mathcal{P}(\cdot\mid x): the worst-case kernel (38) reweights each atom (a,d)(a,d) individually according to the exponentiated continuation value Vr​aκ​(x−a+d)−γ​aV_{ra}^{\kappa}(x-a+d)-\gamma a, and therefore generally lies outside any such parametric family.

Define the regularized continuation branch Qr​aQ_{ra} by capping the likelihood ratio in the uncapped branch Q~r​a\widetilde{Q}_{ra}:

Qr​a(x):=−cx+infℚx∈𝒬κ​(x){𝔼ℚx[Vr​aκ(X^x)−γAx]−1ηDKL(ℚx∥ℙx)}.\displaystyle Q_{ra}(x):=-cx+\inf_{\mathbb{Q}_{x}\in\mathcal{Q}_{\kappa}(x)}\Bigl\{\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}_{x}}\!\bigl[V_{ra}^{\kappa}(\hat{X}_{x})-\gamma A_{x}\bigr]-\frac{1}{\eta}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathbb{Q}_{x}\,\|\,\mathbb{P}_{x})\Bigr\}. (36)

The regularized Bellman equation is then

Vr​aκ​(x)=max⁡{S⁡(x),Qr​a​(x)}.V_{ra}^{\kappa}(x)=\max\!\left\{S(x),\,Q_{ra}(x)\right\}. (37)

We refer to the fixed point of (37) as the regularized value function Vr​aκV_{ra}^{\kappa}.

Theorem 3 (Optimal risk-averse policy under regularization).

Let η<0\eta<0 and κ>1\kappa>1.

  1. (i)

    (Well-posedness) The regularized Bellman equation (37) admits a unique fixed point Vr​aκV_{ra}^{\kappa} in the class of functions u:𝒮→ℝu:\mathcal{S}\to\mathbb{R} satisfying u≥Su\geq S and u⁡(x)≤β​x+Ku(x)\leq\beta x+K for some constant KK; the value iterates V0=SV_{0}=S, Vn+1=𝒯r​a​VnV_{n+1}=\mathcal{T}_{ra}V_{n} increase pointwise to Vr​aκV_{ra}^{\kappa}.

  2. (ii)

    (Threshold optimality) With θr​a∗=min⁡{x:Vr​aκ​(x)=S⁡(x)}\theta^{*}_{ra}=\min\{x:V_{ra}^{\kappa}(x)=S(x)\}, the threshold policy πθr​a∗\pi_{\theta^{*}_{ra}} is optimal among all admissible stopping rules, and Vr​aκV_{ra}^{\kappa} is the value of the robust stopping game. The optimal threshold is unique unless Qr​a​(θr​a∗)=S⁡(θr​a∗)Q_{ra}(\theta^{*}_{ra})=S(\theta^{*}_{ra}), in which case exactly the two adjacent policies πθr​a∗\pi_{\theta^{*}_{ra}} and πθr​a∗+1\pi_{\theta^{*}_{ra}+1} are optimal.

  3. (iii)

    (Worst-case characterization) At every state xx, the infimum in (37) is attained by a unique ℚx∗∈𝒬κ​(x)\mathbb{Q}^{*}_{x}\in\mathcal{Q}_{\kappa}(x), with truncated exponential-tilting likelihood ratio

    d​ℚx∗d​ℙx​(a,d)=min⁡{κ,λx​eη⁡[Vr​aκ​(X^x)−γ​a]},\frac{d\mathbb{Q}^{*}_{x}}{d\mathbb{P}_{x}}(a,d)=\min\!\left\{\kappa,\,\lambda_{x}e^{\eta[V_{ra}^{\kappa}(\hat{X}_{x})-\gamma a]}\right\}, (38)

    where X^x=x−a+d\hat{X}_{x}=x-a+d on the atom (a,d)(a,d), and λx>0\lambda_{x}>0 is chosen so that ℚx∗\mathbb{Q}^{*}_{x} is a probability measure. In particular, ℚx∗\mathbb{Q}^{*}_{x} has full support.

The proof is given in Section 7.

The role and choice of κ\kappa. The likelihood-ratio cap κ\kappa calibrates the amount of model uncertainty against which the decision maker hedges. At κ=1\kappa=1 the uncertainty set (35) collapses to the nominal kernel and the regularized criterion reduces to the risk-neutral one; as κ→∞\kappa\to\infty the likelihood-ratio constraint becomes inactive state-by-state and the capped dual formally approaches the uncapped entropic dual; we use this only as a formal consistency limit, since the uncapped representation is justified here only under the one-step boundedness and exponential-integrability conditions noted above. The next proposition records that the regularized criterion interpolates monotonically—in value and in policy—between these two extremes.

Proposition 7 (Monotonicity and consistency in the robustness bound).

Fix η<0\eta<0 and suppose Assumption 1 holds.

  1. (i)

    (Monotonicity in κ\kappa) The regularized value function Vr​aκ​(x)V_{ra}^{\kappa}(x) is nonincreasing in κ\kappa for every x∈ℤ+x\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}, and the smallest optimal threshold θr​a∗​(κ)\theta^{*}_{ra}(\kappa) is nonincreasing in κ\kappa: a larger uncertainty set strengthens the adversary, depresses the continuation value, and shifts stopping earlier.

  2. (ii)

    (Nominal limit) As κ↓1\kappa\downarrow 1, Vr​aκ​(x)↑Vr​n​(x)V_{ra}^{\kappa}(x)\uparrow V_{rn}(x) for every x∈ℤ+x\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}, and the smallest optimal thresholds coincide for all κ\kappa sufficiently close to 11: there exists κ¯>1\bar{\kappa}>1 such that θr​a∗​(κ)=θr​n∗\theta^{*}_{ra}(\kappa)=\theta^{*}_{rn} for all κ∈(1,κ¯)\kappa\in(1,\bar{\kappa}).

In applications, κ\kappa can be calibrated to the statistical plausibility of alternative models—for instance, as the maximal likelihood ratio between the nominal kernel and the kernels estimated at the boundary of a confidence region for the nominal parameters (p,q)(p,q)—so that the adversary distorts the model only within statistically credible limits; θr​a∗​(κ)\theta^{*}_{ra}(\kappa) then traces out the risk-averse discount as a function of the uncertainty budget (Section 4.5, Figure 5).

Remark 8 (Numerical solution).

The regularized robust Bellman equation (37) is solved numerically by monotone value iteration on a truncated state space, and the ordering of Proposition 8(i) provides the truncation point used in the implementation Xmax:=θr​n∗X_{\max}:=\theta^{*}_{rn}. Implementation details are deferred to Section G.

2.5 Threshold Ordering and Convergence Across Risk Regimes

Proposition 8 (Comparison across risk regimes).

Let δ=1\delta=1, and suppose Assumption 1 holds. For η>0\eta>0, write Vr​s,ηV_{rs,\eta} and θr​s,η∗\theta^{*}_{rs,\eta} for the value function and the smallest optimal threshold of the risk-seeking problem; for η<0\eta<0, write Vr​a,ηκV_{ra,\eta}^{\kappa} for the risk-averse regularized value function and θr​a,η∗\theta^{*}_{ra,\eta} for the optimal threshold of the risk-averse problem, with the robustness parameter κ>1\kappa>1 fixed.

  1. (i)

    (Threshold ordering) The risk-neutral threshold lies between the risk-averse and risk-seeking thresholds:

    θr​a,η′∗≤θr​n∗≤θr​s,η∗,η′<0<η.\theta^{*}_{ra,\eta^{\prime}}\leq\theta^{*}_{rn}\leq\theta^{*}_{rs,\eta},\qquad\eta^{\prime}<0<\eta.
  2. (ii)

    (Risk-seeking limit) For every x∈ℤ+x\in\mathbb{Z}_{+},

    Vr​s,η​(x)↓Vr​n​(x)as ​η↓0.V_{rs,\eta}(x)\downarrow V_{rn}(x)\qquad\text{as }\eta\downarrow 0.

    Moreover, the risk-seeking threshold stabilizes: θr​s,η∗\theta^{*}_{rs,\eta} is constant for all sufficiently small η>0\eta>0, and its limit is an optimal risk-neutral threshold—namely θr​n∗\theta^{*}_{rn} when the undiscounted risk-neutral optimal threshold is unique, and θr​n∗+1\theta^{*}_{rn}+1, the second optimal risk-neutral threshold, in the tie case Δ​f​(θr​n∗)=β\Delta f(\theta^{*}_{rn})=\beta.

  3. (iii)

    (Risk-averse limit) For every x∈ℤ+x\in\mathbb{Z}_{+} and fixed κ>1\kappa>1,

    Vr​a,ηκ​(x)↑Vr​n​(x)as ​η↑0.V_{ra,\eta}^{\kappa}(x)\uparrow V_{rn}(x)\qquad\text{as }\eta\uparrow 0.

    Moreover, there exists η¯<0\underline{\eta}<0 such that

    θr​a,η∗=θr​n∗for all ​η∈(η¯,0):\theta^{*}_{ra,\eta}=\theta^{*}_{rn}\qquad\text{for all }\eta\in(\underline{\eta},0):

    the risk-averse limit always selects the smallest optimal risk-neutral threshold, with no uniqueness assumption required.

3 Extension: Repeated Clearing

In the applications motivating this study—manufacturing transfer batches, order consolidation, packet aggregation, and platelet pooling—clearing is often a recurring event rather than a terminal one: the buffer is emptied, accumulation resumes, and the controller faces the same decision again. Some existing clearing and batch-service literature accordingly adopts long-run average criteria, in contrast to the optimal stopping criteria of Sections 2.2–2.4. This section shows that the first-passage construction of Section 2.2.3 also yields reduced objectives for repeated clearing. The repeated-clearing formulation prices not only the cost accrued within a cycle but also the length of the cycle itself.

Timing convention and regenerative cycles. At the beginning of a period in state xx, the controller may continue or clear. Continuation at discount factor δ\delta incurs the realized holding and abandonment costs c​x+δ​γ​Axcx+\delta\gamma A_{x} and produces the transition X^x=x−Ax+D\hat{X}_{x}=x-A_{x}+D. Clearing is permitted only when x≥1x\geq 1: it generates the terminal reward β​x−α\beta x-\alpha, resets the buffer immediately to 00, and no holding or abandonment cost is charged at the clearing epoch. The next cycle then begins from state 00. Under a stationary clearing policy, the strong Markov property at each clearing epoch makes the cycles independent; under a threshold policy πθ\pi_{\theta}, they are i.i.d. with common length TθT_{\theta}.

For the threshold policy πθ\pi_{\theta}, define the discounted cycle rewards by

Rθ​(δ):=δTθ​(β​θ−α)−∑t=0Tθ−1δt​(c​Xt+δ​γ​At​(Xt)).R_{\theta}(\delta):=\delta^{T_{\theta}}(\beta\theta-\alpha)-\sum_{t=0}^{T_{\theta}-1}\delta^{t}\bigl(cX_{t}+\delta\gamma A_{t}(X_{t})\bigr).

We consider the long-run average reward generated by repeated cycles and the total discounted reward over infinitely many cycles. Let (Tθ,k,Rθ,k​(δ))k≥1(T_{\theta,k},R_{\theta,k}(\delta))_{k\geq 1} be i.i.d. copies of (Tθ,Rθ​(δ))(T_{\theta},R_{\theta}(\delta)), and set S0:=0S_{0}:=0 and Sk:=∑j=1kTθ,jS_{k}:=\sum_{j=1}^{k}T_{\theta,j}. Thus Sk−1S_{k-1} is the clearing epoch at which cycle kk begins.

For δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), the total discounted reward over infinitely many cycles is

Vθ​(δ):=𝔼⁡[∑k=1∞δSk−1​Rθ,k​(δ)]=𝔼​[Rθ​(δ)]1−𝔼⁡[δTθ],V_{\theta}(\delta):=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\delta^{S_{k-1}}R_{\theta,k}(\delta)\right]=\frac{\mathbb{E}[R_{\theta}(\delta)]}{1-\mathbb{E}[\delta^{T_{\theta}}]}, (39)

where independence between the past cycle lengths and the reward in cycle kk gives

𝔼⁡[δSk−1​Rθ,k​(δ)]=(𝔼⁡[δTθ])k−1​𝔼​[Rθ​(δ)].\mathbb{E}\!\left[\delta^{S_{k-1}}R_{\theta,k}(\delta)\right]=\bigl(\mathbb{E}[\delta^{T_{\theta}}]\bigr)^{k-1}\mathbb{E}[R_{\theta}(\delta)].

The geometric series converges because Tθ≥1T_{\theta}\geq 1 and δ<1\delta<1.

For the long-run average criterion, take δ=1\delta=1 within each cycle and define

R¯θ:=limK→∞∑k=1KRθ,k​(1)∑k=1KTθ,k=𝔼​[Rθ​(1)]𝔼⁡[Tθ]a.s.,\overline{R}_{\theta}:=\lim_{K\to\infty}\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{K}R_{\theta,k}(1)}{\sum_{k=1}^{K}T_{\theta,k}}=\frac{\mathbb{E}[R_{\theta}(1)]}{\mathbb{E}[T_{\theta}]}\qquad\text{a.s.}, (40)

provided 𝔼⁡[Tθ]<∞\mathbb{E}[T_{\theta}]<\infty and 𝔼​|Rθ​(1)|<∞\mathbb{E}|R_{\theta}(1)|<\infty. The second equality is the renewal–reward theorem. Hence both criteria reduce to one-cycle calculations: R¯θ>0\overline{R}_{\theta}>0 precisely when 𝔼​[Rθ​(1)]>0\mathbb{E}[R_{\theta}(1)]>0, while Vθ​(δ)>0V_{\theta}(\delta)>0 precisely when 𝔼​[Rθ​(δ)]>0\mathbb{E}[R_{\theta}(\delta)]>0. To distinguish the one-cycle primitives by discount factor, write f⁡(⋅,δ)f(\cdot;\delta) and g⁡(⋅,δ)g(\cdot;\delta) for the functions in Section 2.2.3, and define

Nδ​(θ):=β​θ−α−f⁡(θ,δ).N_{\delta}(\theta):=\beta\theta-\alpha-f(\theta;\delta).

We say that Assumption 1 holds at discount factor δ\delta if Nδ​(θ)>0N_{\delta}(\theta)>0 for some θ≥1\theta\geq 1; since Nδ​(0)=−α<0N_{\delta}(0)=-\alpha<0, quantifying over θ≥1\theta\geq 1 is equivalent to quantifying over θ∈ℤ+\theta\in\mathbb{Z}_{+} used in Section 2.2.4.

Lemma 5 (Time-accumulation function).

Define t:ℤ+→ℝ+t:\mathbb{Z}_{+}\to\mathbb{R}_{+} by t⁡(0)=0t(0)=0 and the forward recurrence

t(x+1)=ωx​t​(x)+1−Ft​(x)(1−p)x​q,Ft(x)=𝔼Ax,D[𝟏{Ax≥1}t(X^x)],t(x+1)=\frac{\omega_{x}\,t(x)+1-F_{t}(x)}{(1-p)^{x}q},\qquad F_{t}(x)=\mathbb{E}_{A_{x},D}\!\left[\mathbf{1}_{\{A_{x}\geq 1\}}\,t(\hat{X}_{x})\right], (41)

where ωx=1−(1−p)x​(1−q)\omega_{x}=1-(1-p)^{x}(1-q). Equivalently, the sequence defined by (41) satisfies

t⁡(x)=−1+𝔼⁡[t⁡(X^x)],x≥0.t(x)=-1+\mathbb{E}\!\left[t(\hat{X}_{x})\right],\qquad x\geq 0. (42)

For every θ≥1\theta\geq 1,

t⁡(θ)=𝔼0​[Tθ].t(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{0}[T_{\theta}]. (43)
Proposition 9 (Repeated-clearing reduced objectives).

Fix θ≥1\theta\geq 1.

  1. (i)

    (Average reward) The long-run average reward of πθ\pi_{\theta} is

    v¯​(θ)=N1​(θ)t⁡(θ).\bar{v}(\theta)=\frac{N_{1}(\theta)}{t(\theta)}. (44)
  2. (ii)

    (Discounted repeated clearing) For δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), the total discounted reward of πθ\pi_{\theta} over infinitely many cycles, started from 00, is

    vδren​(θ)=vr​n​(θ,δ)1−𝔼0​[δTθ]=Nδ​(θ)g⁡(θ,δ)−1.v^{\mathrm{ren}}_{\delta}(\theta)=\frac{v_{rn}(\theta;\delta)}{1-\mathbb{E}_{0}[\delta^{T_{\theta}}]}=\frac{N_{\delta}(\theta)}{g(\theta;\delta)-1}. (45)
  3. (iii)

    (Abelian consistency) For every fixed θ≥1\theta\geq 1,

    (1−δ)​vδren​(θ)⟶v¯​(θ)as ​δ↑1.(1-\delta)\,v^{\mathrm{ren}}_{\delta}(\theta)\longrightarrow\bar{v}(\theta)\qquad\text{as }\delta\uparrow 1. (46)

Parts (i)–(iii) are policy-evaluation identities and require no profitability assumption; Assumption 1 enters only through the optimization results below (Theorem 4 and Proposition 10).

The reduced objectives above evaluate threshold policies. The next proposition records the dynamic-programming step showing that restricting attention to threshold policies entails no loss of optimality for either repeated-clearing criterion.

Proposition 10 (Threshold policies suffice).

Under Assumption 1 at δ=1\delta=1, there exists a threshold policy πθ\pi_{\theta} with θ≥1\theta\geq 1 that is optimal among all stationary clearing policies for the average-reward regenerative problem. The same conclusion holds for the discounted problem at every δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1) at which Assumption 1 holds.

Theorem 4 (Strict unimodality of the repeated-clearing objectives).

Suppose that Assumption 1 holds at the relevant discount factor.

  1. (i)

    (Average reward) The long-run average objective v¯\bar{v} is strictly unimodal over all thresholds θ≥1\theta\geq 1: there exists θ1u≥1\theta^{u}_{1}\geq 1 such that Δ​v¯​(θ)>0\Delta\bar{v}(\theta)>0 for 1≤θ<θ1u1\leq\theta<\theta^{u}_{1}, Δ​v¯​(θ1u)≤0\Delta\bar{v}(\theta^{u}_{1})\leq 0, and Δ​v¯​(θ)<0\Delta\bar{v}(\theta)<0 for θ>θ1u\theta>\theta^{u}_{1}.

  2. (ii)

    (Discounted repeated clearing) For every δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), the objective vδrenv^{\mathrm{ren}}_{\delta} is strictly unimodal over all thresholds θ≥1\theta\geq 1 in the same sense, with crossing index θδu\theta^{u}_{\delta}.

  3. (iii)

    (Optimal thresholds) The indices

    θavg∗=min⁡{θ≥1:Δ​v¯​(θ)≤0},θren∗​(δ)=min⁡{θ≥1:Δ​vδren​(θ)≤0}\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{avg}}=\min\bigl\{\theta\geq 1:\Delta\bar{v}(\theta)\leq 0\bigr\},\qquad\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{ren}}(\delta)=\min\bigl\{\theta\geq 1:\Delta v^{\mathrm{ren}}_{\delta}(\theta)\leq 0\bigr\} (47)

    are well defined and finite, coincide with θ1u\theta^{u}_{1} and θδu\theta^{u}_{\delta}, and are the smallest optimal thresholds for repeated clearing; at most two thresholds are optimal for each criterion, and they differ by one. The corresponding threshold policies are optimal among all stationary clearing policies by Proposition 10.

The proof is given in Section F. Theorem 4 justifies, for both repeated-clearing criteria, the same discrete-ascent procedure that Theorem 1 justifies for the optimal stopping objective: the first local maximizer encountered by a forward pass is the global one.

Remark 9 (Marginal-versus-average interpretation).

The crossing condition compares the average rate with the marginal rate of a one-level cycle extension: Δ​v¯​(θ)≤0\Delta\bar{v}(\theta)\leq 0 exactly when v¯​(θ)≥ξ1​(θ)\bar{v}(\theta)\geq\xi_{1}(\theta), and Δ​vδren​(θ)≤0\Delta v^{\mathrm{ren}}_{\delta}(\theta)\leq 0 exactly when vδren​(θ)≥ξδ​(θ)v^{\mathrm{ren}}_{\delta}(\theta)\geq\xi_{\delta}(\theta) (see (81) in the proof). The marginal rate ξ1​(θ)\xi_{1}(\theta) prices the net reward of extending the cycle from θ\theta to θ+1\theta+1 against the marginal expected cycle length, and its limit −𝒞1q/p-\mathcal{C}_{1}q/p is the negative of the stationary holding-and-abandonment cost rate of the always-continue chain, whose stationary mean inventory level is q/pq/p. The optimal batch size is the first level at which the marginal rate of a larger batch falls below the average rate generated by the current batch—a marginal-versus-average rule in the spirit of classical clearing theory.

The repeated-clearing criteria also sharpen the interpretation of the optimal stopping threshold. Let θr​n∗​(1)\theta^{*}_{rn}(1) and θr​n∗​(δ)\theta^{*}_{rn}(\delta) denote the smallest optimal stopping thresholds at δ=1\delta=1 and at δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), respectively.

Proposition 11.

Suppose that Assumption 1 holds. The smallest optimal thresholds for repeated clearing satisfy

θavg∗≤θr​n∗​(1),θren∗​(δ)≤θr​n∗​(δ).\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{avg}}\leq\theta^{*}_{rn}(1),\qquad\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{ren}}(\delta)\leq\theta^{*}_{rn}(\delta). (48)
Remark 10.

The optimal stopping objective prices erosion within a single cycle. The repeated-clearing objectives additionally price the opportunity cost of the cycle length through t⁡(θ)t(\theta) in (44) and through g⁡(θ,δ)−1g(\theta;\delta)-1 in (45). Proposition 11 formalizes the resulting over-batching bias: the optimal stopping threshold is an upper bound on the corresponding repeated-clearing threshold.

Remark 11 (Entropic criteria).

The additive cycle-reward reduction is specific to additive criteria. Under an entropic criterion, cycle rewards combine multiplicatively, so i.i.d. cycles do not yield the scalar formulas (44) and (45). A risk-sensitive theory for repeated clearing would require an ergodic multiplicative-functional or recursive-entropic formulation (Borkar and Meyn 2002); we do not pursue that extension in this paper.

4 Numerical Study

4.1 Experimental Design and Baseline Calibration

Baseline parameters. The baseline is chosen so that the profitability condition (20) holds with a nontrivial optimal threshold, the buffer displays appreciable stochastic variability, and the three risk regimes admit interior, mutually comparable solutions. Unless otherwise stated, every experiment below fixes the baseline parameters of Table 1; the table also reports the grid ranges used in the comparison and sensitivity experiments.

Solution procedures.

  1. (a)

    Risk-neutral forward recursion: forward iteration of (10)–(12), followed by the discrete ascent on vr​nv_{rn} justified by Theorem 1.

  2. (b)

    Risk-seeking forward recursion: forward iteration of (27), terminated at the first index satisfying Δ​fr​s​(θ)≥β\Delta f_{rs}(\theta)\geq\beta, per Theorem 2.

  3. (c)

    Regularized risk-averse value iteration: monotone value iteration of the robust operator in (37), initialized at the stopping reward and truncated at Xmax=θr​n∗X_{\max}=\theta^{*}_{rn} per Proposition 8(i), with the inner Donsker–Varadhan dual solved by bisection on log⁡λx\log\lambda_{x} (Section G).

  4. (d)

    Repeated-clearing forward recursion: forward iteration of (10)–(12) at the relevant discount factor and, for the average-reward criterion, of the time-accumulation recursion (41), followed by a discrete ascent on the repeated-clearing objectives (44) and (45) terminated at the first nonpositive marginal improvement, per Theorem 4.

All computations are performed in double precision; convergence tolerances and truncation rules are reported with each experiment.

4.2 Sensitivity to the Economic Primitives

Starting from the baseline, we vary one primitive at a time over the grid ranges reported in Table 1, holding all remaining parameters fixed. Figure 1 reports comparative statics for the optimal risk-neutral threshold θr​n∗\theta^{*}_{rn} with respect to the seven primitives. The optimal threshold increases with the stopping cost α\alpha—from θr​n∗=43\theta^{*}_{rn}=43 at the baseline to 9191 at α=1000\alpha=1000—because larger fixed costs require larger batches for amortization (Lemma 21(ii)). It decreases with the holding cost cc and the abandonment penalty γ\gamma, both of which raise the effective cost of accumulation (Lemma 21(i)), and with the abandonment probability pp, which additionally steepens the downward drift. It increases with the arrival probability qq, which raises the upward drift of the inventory process.

The response to δ\delta is strong: θr​n∗\theta^{*}_{rn} rises from 1616 at δ=0.9\delta=0.9 to 7373 at δ=1\delta=1, as greater patience lowers the opportunity cost of extending accumulation. The sign of the response in the β\beta panel is not determined by cost monotonicity alone: at the baseline δ=0.99\delta=0.99, the threshold decreases from 5353 at β=1\beta=1 to 4141 at β=100\beta=100. The sign of this response is governed by a reward–discount phase transition, discussed in Section H.1.

4.3 Operational Implications

We illustrate the factorization of the discounted reduced objective from Remark 2 and discuss its operational content. Recall that

vr​n​(θ)=Nr​n​(θ)​𝔼​[δTθ]=β​θ−α−f⁡(θ)g⁡(θ),v_{rn}(\theta)=N_{rn}(\theta)\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\delta^{T_{\theta}}\right]=\frac{\beta\theta-\alpha-f(\theta)}{g(\theta)},

where Nr​n​(θ)=β​θ−α−f⁡(θ)N_{rn}(\theta)=\beta\theta-\alpha-f(\theta) and 𝔼⁡[δTθ]=1/g⁡(θ)\mathbb{E}[\delta^{T_{\theta}}]=1/g(\theta). In Figure 2(a), the accrued nominal value Nr​n​(θ)N_{rn}(\theta) rises almost linearly at first—the reward coefficient β\beta dominates the accumulating holding and abandonment costs—peaks at approximately 381381 near θ=61\theta=61, and then declines, crossing zero between θ=78\theta=78 and θ=79\theta=79: beyond that point, accrued costs outweigh the batch reward even before discounting. Over the same range, the expected discount factor 𝔼⁡[δTθ]\mathbb{E}[\delta^{T_{\theta}}] falls from 11 to below 0.050.05. The optimum θr​n∗=43\theta^{*}_{rn}=43 therefore lies well inside the region where nominal accrual is still increasing: discount erosion binds before cost accrual does. At the optimum, the policy accrues nominal value Nr​n​(43)≈295N_{rn}(43)\approx 295; waiting erodes more than half of it, with 𝔼⁡[δT43]≈0.47\mathbb{E}[\delta^{T_{43}}]\approx 0.47, leaving vr​n​(43)≈138v_{rn}(43)\approx 138.

Figure 2(b) reports the simulated distribution of the batching cycle TθT_{\theta} under πθ\pi_{\theta} for θ∈{21,43,64}\theta\in\{21,43,64\}, using 10510^{5} independent paths per threshold. The mean cycle length grows faster than the threshold: halving θr​n∗\theta^{*}_{rn} from 4343 to 2121 shortens the mean cycle from 7676 to 3030 periods, whereas raising it to 6464 lengthens the mean to 155155. The mechanism is the abandonment hazard: as inventory accumulates, abandonment drains the net drift q−p​𝔼​[Xt]q-p\,\mathbb{E}[X_{t}], so the chain climbs more slowly the higher it must go. Over-batching is therefore disproportionately expensive in capital lock-up, a convexity that the scalar objective alone does not display.

4.4 The Risk-Seeking Premium and the Risk-Averse Discount

This subsection compares the three criteria under the undiscounted calibration δ=1\delta=1 of Assumption 2. We define the risk-seeking premium as θr​s∗−θr​n∗\theta^{*}_{rs}-\theta^{*}_{rn} and the risk-averse discount as θr​n∗−θr​a∗\theta^{*}_{rn}-\theta^{*}_{ra}. Figure 3 summarizes the comparison: panel (a) traces the three thresholds as functions of pp, and panel (b) tracks the risk-adjusted thresholds as η→0\eta\to 0; the ordering is that of Proposition 8(i). Throughout, θr​a∗\theta^{*}_{ra} is computed under the regularized criterion of Section 2.4 at a fixed cap κ\kappa, reported in each figure.

Risk-seeking premium (η>0\eta>0). The entropic tilt deflates the marginal accumulation cost pointwise, Δ​fr​s​(θ)≤Δ​f​(θ)\Delta f_{rs}(\theta)\leq\Delta f(\theta) (Proposition 13(ii)), shifting the first crossing of the marginal-cost curve with the reward coefficient β\beta to the right: at the undiscounted calibration, the crossing moves from θr​n∗=73\theta^{*}_{rn}=73 to θr​s∗=92,116,141,195\theta^{*}_{rs}=92,116,141,195 as η\eta ranges over {0.05,0.10,0.15,0.25}\{0.05,0.10,0.15,0.25\} (Figure 4(a)).

Risk-averse discount (η<0\eta<0). Because the robust inner optimization destroys the scalar forward recursion available in the risk-seeking case, the threshold is characterized through the stopping gap Vr​aκ​(x)−S⁡(x)V^{\kappa}_{ra}(x)-S(x) rather than through a marginal-cost crossing; Figure 4(b) shows that the gap is positive on the continuation region and closes at the optimal threshold. As |η||\eta| grows, the gap closes earlier: at κ=5\kappa=5, the first zero moves from θr​n∗=73\theta^{*}_{rn}=73 to θr​a∗=51,42,27,14\theta^{*}_{ra}=51,42,27,14 for η∈{−0.05,−0.10,−0.20,−0.50}\eta\in\{-0.05,-0.10,-0.20,-0.50\}.

Continuity at η=0\eta=0. Figure 3(b) confirms the threshold continuity of Proposition 8(ii)–(iii): the risk-averse threshold approaches θr​n∗\theta^{*}_{rn} from below as η↑0\eta\uparrow 0, the risk-seeking threshold approaches it from above as η↓0\eta\downarrow 0, and the two coincide with θr​n∗\theta^{*}_{rn} for sufficiently small |η||\eta| on the reported grid.

4.5 Worst-Case Distortion of the Abandonment Distribution

Figure 5 visualizes the adversary’s optimal distortion of the abandonment distribution at the representative state x=30x=30, with p=0.04p=0.04 and η=−0.3\eta=-0.3. The left panel compares the nominal abandonment PMF ℙx(A)\mathbb{P}^{(A)}_{x} with the abandonment marginals ℚx∗,(A)\mathbb{Q}^{*,(A)}_{x} of the robust joint laws ℚx∗\mathbb{Q}^{*}_{x} for likelihood-ratio caps κ∈{1.5,3.0,5.0}\kappa\in\{1.5,3.0,5.0\}. As κ\kappa increases, the adversary shifts more mass toward the right tail, increasing the weight on severe abandonment events and lowering the continuation value.

The right panel plots the likelihood ratio of the abandonment marginal, d​ℚx∗,(A)/d​ℙx(A)d\mathbb{Q}^{*,(A)}_{x}/d\mathbb{P}^{(A)}_{x}, against the abandonment count aa; it is obtained by averaging the joint truncated tilt (38) over the arrival atom dd. The profile has two phases: an exponentially tilted region and a capped region. High-abandonment atoms are scaled up until the likelihood ratio reaches κ\kappa, after which the constraint binds and the ratio is flat. The active constraints at κ=1.5,3.0,5.0\kappa=1.5,3.0,5.0 show how the cap limits the pessimism that the adversary can introduce.

4.6 Repeated-Clearing Calibration

Table 2 contrasts the optimal stopping and repeated-clearing optima at the baseline calibration. The repeated-clearing thresholds are computed by the discrete ascent of Theorem 4. For comparability, the discounted repeated-clearing objective is reported in average-equivalent form, (1−δ)​vδren​(θ)(1-\delta)v^{\mathrm{ren}}_{\delta}(\theta), so that the optimal values in both columns are measured per period.

As an internal consistency check, the analytical mean cycle lengths agree with the simulated means in Figure 2(b): t⁡(43)=76.1t(43)=76.1 and t⁡(64)=155.0t(64)=155.0, compared with simulated means of approximately 7676 and 155155, respectively. Using the optimal stopping threshold rather than the corresponding repeated-clearing optimum sacrifices 47.6%47.6\% of the attainable average reward and 18.3%18.3\% of the average-equivalent discounted repeated-clearing value at δ=0.99\delta=0.99.

Proofs of the supporting results are deferred to Section C.

  2. (ii)

    Δ​fr​s​(θ)≤Δ​f​(θ)\Delta f_{rs}(\theta)\leq\Delta f(\theta) for all θ\theta;

  3. (iii)

    Under Assumption 1, θr​s∗≥θr​n∗\theta^{*}_{rs}\geq\theta^{*}_{rn}: the risk-seeking threshold is no smaller than the undiscounted risk-neutral threshold of Theorem 1.

Proposition 14 (Strict convexity of fr​sf_{rs}).

For all θ≥0\theta\geq 0, Δ2​fr​s​(θ)≥c\Delta^{2}f_{rs}(\theta)\geq c. In particular, fr​sf_{rs} is strictly convex, Δ​fr​s​(θ)≥c​θ\Delta f_{rs}(\theta)\geq c\theta, and fr​s​(θ)≥c​θ​(θ−1)/2f_{rs}(\theta)\geq c\,\theta(\theta-1)/2.

Proof of Theorem 2.

By Proposition 6, some threshold policy is optimal among all admissible policies, so it suffices to maximize vr​s​(θ)=β​θ−α−fr​s​(θ)v_{rs}(\theta)=\beta\theta-\alpha-f_{rs}(\theta) over θ∈ℤ+\theta\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}.

The remaining claims restate Proposition 6: Vr​s​(0)=vr​s​(θr​s∗)=maxθ≥0⁡vr​s​(θ)V_{rs}(0)=v_{rs}(\theta^{*}_{rs})=\max_{\theta\geq 0}v_{rs}(\theta), and πθr​s∗\pi_{\theta^{*}_{rs}} is optimal among all admissible policies. ∎

This section proves Theorem 3: Lemma 11 establishes a uniform Foster–Lyapunov drift condition over the adversary’s measures, Lemmas 12–13 and Proposition 15 give attainment, full support, and monotone value iteration, Lemma 14 and Corollary 1 yield the threshold structure, Lemma 15 gives uniqueness, and Proposition 16 identifies the fixed point with the robust game value. At δ=1\delta=1, the corresponding risk-neutral operator is

𝒯r​a​u≤𝒯r​n​u,u≥S.\mathcal{T}_{ra}u\leq\mathcal{T}_{rn}u,\qquad u\geq S. (54)

There is a constant Cκ>0C_{\kappa}>0 such that, for every x∈ℤ+x\in\mathbb{Z}_{+} and every ℚx∈𝒬κ​(x)\mathbb{Q}_{x}\in\mathcal{Q}_{\kappa}(x),

Lemma 12 (Attainment of the one-step robust infimum).

Let ℙ\mathbb{P} be a probability measure with full support on a finite set 𝒳\mathcal{X}, and let κ>1\kappa>1. The one-step robust operator

ℛ(Z)=infℚ∈𝒬κ{𝔼ℚ[Z]−1ηDKL(ℚ∥ℙ)},Z∈ℝ𝒳,\mathcal{R}(Z)=\inf_{\mathbb{Q}\in\mathcal{Q}_{\kappa}}\Bigl\{\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}[Z]-\frac{1}{\eta}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathbb{Q}\,\|\,\mathbb{P})\Bigr\},\quad Z\in\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{X}},

8 Concluding Remarks

We have developed a methodology for optimal batch clearing with item-level abandonment, combining threshold verification with forward first-passage recursions. The approach explicitly characterizes optimal policies under risk-neutral, risk-seeking, and regularized risk-averse criteria, as well as under repeated-clearing objectives, and identifies the worst-case transition law in truncated-Gibbs form. More broadly, the analysis shows that attrition couples batch size to cycle duration, making delay, risk posture, and repeated operation integral to optimal batching decisions.

Our results carry several implications for the management of batch clearing systems. First, the optimal clearing rule is simple to implement: process the batch as soon as the inventory reaches a directly computable threshold. The threshold moves in the intuitive directions—it increases with the stopping cost and the arrival probability and decreases with the holding cost, the abandonment penalty, and the abandonment probability—so attrition-prone environments call for smaller, more frequent batches. Second, at the optimum it is time, not cost, that binds: the nominal value of the batch is still increasing when clearing is triggered, and what forces the decision is the erosion of that value while waiting. Because abandonment can slow accumulation progressively as the buffer grows, over-batching is disproportionately expensive—cycle lengths grow superlinearly in the threshold—so when in doubt, managers should favor smaller batches. Third, risk posture enters the decision as an explicit, priced adjustment: risk seeking deflates the perceived marginal cost of accumulation and justifies a larger batch—the risk-seeking premium—whereas risk aversion acts as insurance against abandonment-heavy distortions of the model, with the likelihood-ratio cap bounding how pessimistic the hedge may become and the resulting risk-averse discount quantifying the price of that protection.

Several directions for future research follow. On the modeling side, positive service times, capacity constraints, partial batches, compound arrivals, multiple item classes under joint capacity constraints, and nonstationary arrival dynamics are natural extensions, with applications to perishable-goods logistics and cloud task aggregation. On the methodological side, the discounted entropic criterion requires an augmented-state analysis; a discounted recursive entropic criterion is different again and is treated separately in Section A. A risk-sensitive renewal theory is a further open direction: under an entropic criterion, cycle rewards combine multiplicatively, so the additive renewal–reward reduction does not apply and an ergodic multiplicative-functional or recursive-entropic formulation would be required. The robust dual formulation also suggests a distributionally robust version with parameters learned online and the likelihood-ratio cap calibrated from data. More generally, the two-step strategy used here—a uniform increments bound to isolate the threshold family, followed by a first-passage decomposition—extends beyond the present cost structure; identifying further classes of controlled skip-free processes in which it yields exact reduced objectives may be of independent interest.
