Appendix

Section A presents two formulations of the discounted risk-sensitive problem, for which the exact decomposition no longer applies, together with numerical validation. Sections B–D collect the supporting proofs for the risk-neutral, risk-seeking, and risk-averse analyses. Section E proves Proposition 8, and Section F provides the proofs supporting the renewal formulation of Section 3. Section G states the exact computational algorithms induced by the threshold characterizations, while Section H develops the comparative statics of the optimal risk-neutral threshold, including the reward–discount phase transition underlying Section 4.

Appendix A Discounted Risk-Sensitive Formulations

This section develops the two discounted extensions of the entropic criterion announced in Remark 4. Throughout, let δ<1\delta<1. For an admissible stopping time τ\tau, define the discounted reward by

ℛδ​(τ)=δτ​(β​Xτ−α)−∑t=0τ−1δt​(c​Xt+δ​γ​At​(Xt)),\mathcal{R}_{\delta}(\tau)\;=\;\delta^{\tau}(\beta X_{\tau}-\alpha)-\sum_{t=0}^{\tau-1}\delta^{t}\bigl(cX_{t}+\delta\gamma A_{t}(X_{t})\bigr),

so that Jr​n​(x,τ)=𝔼x​[ℛδ​(τ)]J_{rn}(x,\tau)=\mathbb{E}_{x}[\mathcal{R}_{\delta}(\tau)] and Jr​(x,τ)=η−1​log⁡𝔼x​[eη​ℛδ​(τ)]J_{r}(x,\tau)=\eta^{-1}\log\mathbb{E}_{x}[e^{\eta\mathcal{R}_{\delta}(\tau)}].

Lemma 16 (Deterministic bounds under discounting).

For every x∈𝒮x\in\mathcal{S} and every admissible τ\tau, with t¯:=maxt≥0⁡t​δt≤(e​|log⁡δ|)−1\bar{t}:=\max_{t\geq 0}t\delta^{t}\leq(e|\log\delta|)^{-1},

−α−(c+δ​γ)​(x1−δ+δ(1−δ)2)≤ℛδ​(τ)≤β⁡(x+t¯)ℙx​-a.s.\displaystyle-\alpha-(c+\delta\gamma)\Bigl(\frac{x}{1-\delta}+\frac{\delta}{(1-\delta)^{2}}\Bigr)\;\leq\;\mathcal{R}_{\delta}(\tau)\;\leq\;\beta\,(x+\bar{t})\qquad\mathbb{P}_{x}\text{-a.s.} (56)

Consequently, 𝔼x​[eη​ℛδ​(τ)]\mathbb{E}_{x}[e^{\eta\mathcal{R}_{\delta}(\tau)}] is finite for every η∈ℝ\eta\in\mathbb{R}, x∈𝒮x\in\mathcal{S}, and every admissible τ\tau: under discounting, no exponential-moment restriction is required for either sign of η\eta. The undiscounted case differs not because the value diverges, but because no discount modulus is available and the unregularized continuation branch lacks uniform control.

Proof of Lemma 16.

Since Xt+1−Xt≤Dt≤1X_{t+1}-X_{t}\leq D_{t}\leq 1 almost surely, Xt≤x+tX_{t}\leq x+t and At​(Xt)≤XtA_{t}(X_{t})\leq X_{t} for all tt. The lower bound follows by summing ∑t≥0δt​(x+t)=x/(1−δ)+δ/(1−δ)2\sum_{t\geq 0}\delta^{t}(x+t)=x/(1-\delta)+\delta/(1-\delta)^{2}; the upper bound follows from δτ​(β​Xτ−α)≤β​δτ​(x+τ)≤β⁡(x+t¯)\delta^{\tau}(\beta X_{\tau}-\alpha)\leq\beta\,\delta^{\tau}(x+\tau)\leq\beta(x+\bar{t}). ∎

A.1 Method A: Risk-Parameter Augmentation

For λ≠0\lambda\neq 0, define

𝒲⁡(x,λ)=optτ∈𝔗𝔼x​[eλ​ℛδ​(τ)],opt={sup,λ>0,inf,λ<0.\mathcal{W}(x,\lambda)\;=\;\operatorname*{opt}_{\tau\in\mathfrak{T}}\,\mathbb{E}_{x}\!\bigl[e^{\lambda\mathcal{R}_{\delta}(\tau)}\bigr],\qquad\operatorname*{opt}=\begin{cases}\sup,&\lambda>0,\\ \inf,&\lambda<0.\end{cases}
Proposition 17 (Augmented Bellman recursion).

For every x∈𝒮x\in\mathcal{S} and λ≠0\lambda\neq 0,

𝒲⁡(x,λ)=opt{eλ⁡(β​x−α),𝔼⁡[e−λ⁡(c​x+δ​γ​Ax)​𝒲​(X^x,λ​δ)]},\displaystyle\mathcal{W}(x,\lambda)\;=\;\operatorname*{opt}\Bigl\{\,e^{\lambda(\beta x-\alpha)},\mathbb{E}\!\bigl[e^{-\lambda(cx+\delta\gamma A_{x})}\,\mathcal{W}(\hat{X}_{x},\,\lambda\delta)\bigr]\Bigr\}, (57)

and the discounted entropic value is

Jδr​(x)\displaystyle J^{r}_{\delta}(x) :=supτ∈𝔗η−1​log⁡𝔼x​[eη​ℛδ​(τ)]=η−1​log⁡𝒲⁡(x,η).\displaystyle:=\sup_{\tau\in\mathfrak{T}}\,\eta^{-1}\log\mathbb{E}_{x}\bigl[e^{\eta\mathcal{R}_{\delta}(\tau)}\bigr]=\eta^{-1}\log\mathcal{W}(x,\eta).
Proof of Proposition 17.

Condition on the first period. If τ=0\tau=0, the reward is β​x−α\beta x-\alpha; if τ≥1\tau\geq 1, write ℛδ​(τ)=−(c​X0+δ​γ​A0)+δ​ℛδ′\mathcal{R}_{\delta}(\tau)=-(cX_{0}+\delta\gamma A_{0})+\delta\mathcal{R}_{\delta}^{\prime}, where, conditionally on (A0,D0)(A_{0},D_{0}), ℛδ′\mathcal{R}_{\delta}^{\prime} is distributed as ℛδ​(τ−1)\mathcal{R}_{\delta}(\tau-1) under the initial state X1=X^xX_{1}=\hat{X}_{x}. Factoring the deterministic term out of the exponential and taking opt\operatorname*{opt} over the continuation and then over the first-period decision yields (57); the interchange is the optimality principle for exponential-utility control [Chung and Sobel, 1987], whose moment assumptions hold by Lemma 16. For λ<0\lambda<0, the branches combine by inf\inf because w↦λ−1​log⁡ww\mapsto\lambda^{-1}\log w is decreasing; equivalently, the certainty equivalent is always maximized over τ\tau, since this decreasing map turns minimization of 𝔼⁡[eλ​ℛδ]\mathbb{E}[e^{\lambda\mathcal{R}_{\delta}}] into maximization of its certainty equivalent. ∎

The recursion (57) is the stopping-problem special case of the discounted exponential-utility dynamic program of Chung and Sobel [1987] (cf. Denardo and Rothblum, 1979, Bouakiz and Sobel, 1992). The effective risk sensitivity at period tt is η​δt\eta\delta^{t}: the decision maker becomes asymptotically risk-neutral, and the optimal rule is stationary in the augmented state (x,η​δt)(x,\eta\delta^{t}) but generally not a fixed threshold in xx. The threshold structure is nonetheless retained: for η>0\eta>0 the optimal rule remains a control limit—now a moving boundary x∗​(η​δt)x^{*}(\eta\delta^{t})—that converges to the risk-neutral threshold as the effective risk sensitivity vanishes (Proposition 18).

Proposition 18 (Boundary form of the optimal policy, η>0\eta>0).

Let η>0\eta>0 and Vλ​(x):=λ−1​log⁡𝒲⁡(x,λ)V_{\lambda}(x):=\lambda^{-1}\log\mathcal{W}(x,\lambda). Then:

  1. (i)

    Vλ​(x+1)−Vλ​(x)≤βV_{\lambda}(x+1)-V_{\lambda}(x)\leq\beta for all x≥0x\geq 0 and λ∈(0,η]\lambda\in(0,\eta];

  2. (ii)

    the stopping region 𝒮∗​(λ):={x:𝒲⁡(x,λ)=eλ⁡(β​x−α)}\mathcal{S}^{*}(\lambda):=\{x:\mathcal{W}(x,\lambda)=e^{\lambda(\beta x-\alpha)}\} is nonempty and up-closed; writing x∗​(λ):=min⁡𝒮∗​(λ)x^{*}(\lambda):=\min\mathcal{S}^{*}(\lambda), the policy that stops at the first tt with Xt≥x∗​(η​δt)X_{t}\geq x^{*}(\eta\delta^{t}) is optimal;

  3. (iii)

    x∗​(λ)→θr​n∗x^{*}(\lambda)\to\theta^{*}_{rn} as λ↓0\lambda\downarrow 0 whenever the optimal discounted risk-neutral threshold θr​n∗\theta^{*}_{rn} of Theorem 1 is unique; in the tie case Δ​vr​n​(θr​n∗)=0\Delta v_{rn}(\theta^{*}_{rn})=0, x∗​(λ)∈{θr​n∗,θr​n∗+1}x^{*}(\lambda)\in\{\theta^{*}_{rn},\theta^{*}_{rn}+1\} for all sufficiently small λ\lambda (both elements are optimal risk-neutral thresholds).

Proof of Proposition 18.

(i) Couple two copies started at x+1x+1 and xx as in Lemma 3: the gap ζt∈{0,1}\zeta_{t}\in\{0,1\} satisfies ζt+1=ζt−Bt\zeta_{t+1}=\zeta_{t}-B_{t}, Bt∼Binomial⁡(ζt,p)B_{t}\sim\mathrm{Binomial}(\zeta_{t},p), and for every stopping time τ\tau applied to both copies,

ℛδx+1−ℛδx=δτ​β​ζτ−∑t=0τ−1δt​(c​ζt+δ​γ​Bt)≤βa.s.,\mathcal{R}_{\delta}^{x+1}-\mathcal{R}_{\delta}^{x}\;=\;\delta^{\tau}\beta\zeta_{\tau}-\sum_{t=0}^{\tau-1}\delta^{t}\bigl(c\zeta_{t}+\delta\gamma B_{t}\bigr)\;\leq\;\beta\quad\text{a.s.},

because δτ​β​ζτ≤β\delta^{\tau}\beta\zeta_{\tau}\leq\beta and the cost gap is nonnegative. For λ>0\lambda>0 this gives eλ​ℛδx+1≤eλ​β​eλ​ℛδxe^{\lambda\mathcal{R}_{\delta}^{x+1}}\leq e^{\lambda\beta}e^{\lambda\mathcal{R}_{\delta}^{x}} pathwise; taking expectations, applying λ−1​log\lambda^{-1}\log, and then taking the supremum over τ\tau yields (i).

(ii) Immediate stopping gives Vλ​(x+1)≥β⁡(x+1)−αV_{\lambda}(x+1)\geq\beta(x+1)-\alpha; if x∈𝒮∗​(λ)x\in\mathcal{S}^{*}(\lambda), then by (i), Vλ​(x+1)≤Vλ​(x)+β=β⁡(x+1)−αV_{\lambda}(x+1)\leq V_{\lambda}(x)+\beta=\beta(x+1)-\alpha, hence equality and x+1∈𝒮∗​(λ)x+1\in\mathcal{S}^{*}(\lambda). For nonemptiness, continuing from xx at least one period yields at most −c​x+δ​β​(x+1+t¯)-cx+\delta\beta(x+1+\bar{t}) pathwise (the first-period holding cost plus the reward bound of Lemma 16 from x+1x+1), versus β​x−α\beta x-\alpha from stopping; the difference x⁡(c+β⁡(1−δ))−α−δ​β​(1+t¯)→∞x\bigl(c+\beta(1-\delta)\bigr)-\alpha-\delta\beta(1+\bar{t})\to\infty, so stopping is strictly optimal at all large xx. Optimality of the first-entrance rule follows from the one-step look-ahead property of the Snell envelope, as in Proposition 6.

(iii) By Lemma 16, |ℛδ​(τ)|≤B⁡(x,δ)|\mathcal{R}_{\delta}(\tau)|\leq B(x,\delta) for a deterministic B⁡(x,δ)B(x,\delta), uniformly over admissible τ\tau and for almost every path, so the cumulant expansion

1λ​log⁡𝔼x​[eλ​ℛδ​(τ)]=𝔼x​[ℛδ​(τ)]+λ2​Varx⁡(ℛδ​(τ))+O⁡(λ2)\frac{1}{\lambda}\log\mathbb{E}_{x}\!\left[e^{\lambda\mathcal{R}_{\delta}(\tau)}\right]=\mathbb{E}_{x}[\mathcal{R}_{\delta}(\tau)]+\frac{\lambda}{2}\,\operatorname{Var}_{x}\!\bigl(\mathcal{R}_{\delta}(\tau)\bigr)+O(\lambda^{2})

holds uniformly over τ\tau, with Varx⁡(ℛδ​(τ))≤B​(x,δ)2\operatorname{Var}_{x}(\mathcal{R}_{\delta}(\tau))\leq B(x,\delta)^{2}; taking the supremum over τ\tau yields Vλ​(x)=Vr​n​(x)+O⁡(λ)V_{\lambda}(x)=V_{rn}(x)+O(\lambda) for each fixed xx, where Vr​nV_{rn} is the discounted risk-neutral value of Section 2.2.

For the lower bound, Theorem 1(iii) gives Vr​n​(x)>S​(x)V_{rn}(x)>S(x) at every x<θr​n∗x<\theta^{*}_{rn}; the expansion is uniform on the finite set {0,…,θr​n∗−1}\{0,\dots,\theta^{*}_{rn}-1\}, so Vλ​(x)>S​(x)V_{\lambda}(x)>S(x) there for small λ\lambda, and x∗​(λ)≥θr​n∗x^{*}(\lambda)\geq\theta^{*}_{rn}.

For the upper bound, let Vr​ncont​(x):=−𝒞​x+δ​𝔼​[Vr​n​(X^x)]V^{\mathrm{cont}}_{rn}(x):=-\mathcal{C}x+\delta\,\mathbb{E}[V_{rn}(\hat{X}_{x})] and Λ⁡(x):=S⁡(x)−Vr​ncont​(x)\Lambda(x):=S(x)-V^{\mathrm{cont}}_{rn}(x); the dynamic programming principle gives 𝔼x​[ℛδ​(τ)]≤Vr​ncont​(x)\mathbb{E}_{x}[\mathcal{R}_{\delta}(\tau)]\leq V^{\mathrm{cont}}_{rn}(x) for every τ≥1\tau\geq 1. By Lemma 10, Λ\Lambda is nonnegative and nondecreasing for x≥θr​n∗x\geq\theta^{*}_{rn}. In the unique-maximizer case, Δ​vr​n​(θr​n∗)<0\Delta v_{rn}(\theta^{*}_{rn})<0, so the increment formula for Λ\Lambda gives Λ⁡(θr​n∗)>0\Lambda(\theta^{*}_{rn})>0, and monotonicity gives Λ⁡(x)>0\Lambda(x)>0 for every x≥θr​n∗x\geq\theta^{*}_{rn}. In the tie case, Λ⁡(θr​n∗)=0\Lambda(\theta^{*}_{rn})=0, but h⁡(θr​n∗+2)>0h(\theta^{*}_{rn}+2)>0 and the upward transition from θr​n∗+1\theta^{*}_{rn}+1 has positive probability; hence the expectation formula for Λ\Lambda gives Λ⁡(θr​n∗+1)>0\Lambda(\theta^{*}_{rn}+1)>0, and again Λ⁡(x)>0\Lambda(x)>0 for every x≥θr​n∗+1x\geq\theta^{*}_{rn}+1. With εx:=Λ⁡(x)>0\varepsilon_{x}:=\Lambda(x)>0 on the relevant range, every τ≥1\tau\geq 1 satisfies

1λ​log⁡𝔼x​[eλ​ℛδ​(τ)]≤S⁡(x)−εx+λ2​B​(x,δ)2+O⁡(λ2)<S⁡(x)\frac{1}{\lambda}\log\mathbb{E}_{x}\!\left[e^{\lambda\mathcal{R}_{\delta}(\tau)}\right]\;\leq\;S(x)-\varepsilon_{x}+\frac{\lambda}{2}\,B(x,\delta)^{2}+O(\lambda^{2})\;<\;S(x)

for all sufficiently small λ\lambda, so stopping is strictly optimal at xx. Hence x∗​(λ)≤θr​n∗x^{*}(\lambda)\leq\theta^{*}_{rn} in the unique-maximizer case and x∗​(λ)≤θr​n∗+1x^{*}(\lambda)\leq\theta^{*}_{rn}+1 in the tie case; together with the lower bound, this proves the claim. ∎

Remark 12 (Computation).

Equation (57) is solved by backward recursion on λk=η​δk\lambda_{k}=\eta\delta^{k}, using the terminal approximation 𝒲⁡(x,λK)=eλK​Vr​n​(x)+O⁡(λK2)\mathcal{W}(x,\lambda_{K})=e^{\lambda_{K}V_{rn}(x)}+O(\lambda_{K}^{2}) from Proposition 18(iii); each step requires one finite expectation over (Ax,D)(A_{x},D) (validated in Section A.3).

A.2 Method B: Stationary Bellman

If instead the entropic measure is applied period by period, the Bellman equation is (26) with δ\delta inside the exponent:

Vr​sδ​(x)=max⁡{β​x−α,Qr​sδ​(x)},whereQr​sδ​(x):=−c​x+1η​log⁡𝔼⁡[eη​δ​(Vr​sδ​(X^x)−γ​Ax)].V^{\delta}_{rs}(x)=\max\Bigl\{\beta x-\alpha,\;Q^{\delta}_{rs}(x)\Bigr\},\quad\text{where}\quad Q^{\delta}_{rs}(x):=-cx+\frac{1}{\eta}\log\mathbb{E}\!\Bigl[e^{\eta\delta\bigl(V^{\delta}_{rs}(\hat{X}_{x})-\gamma A_{x}\bigr)}\Bigr]. (58)
Proposition 19.

Let η≠0\eta\neq 0 and let 𝒯r​sδ\mathcal{T}^{\delta}_{rs} denote the operator on the right-hand side of (58).

  1. (i)

    On the truncated state space {0,…,Xmax}\{0,\dots,X_{\max}\} with stopping imposed at XmaxX_{\max}, 𝒯r​sδ\mathcal{T}^{\delta}_{rs} is a supremum-norm contraction with modulus δ\delta. On the untruncated space, for every ρ∈(1,1/δ)\rho\in(1,1/\delta), it is a contraction on ℬρ\mathcal{B}_{\rho} with modulus δ​ρ\delta\rho; hence (58) has a unique fixed point in ℬρ\mathcal{B}_{\rho} and value iteration converges geometrically. Moreover, the fixed point satisfies S⁡(x)≤Vr​sδ​(x)≤β​x+KδS(x)\leq V^{\delta}_{rs}(x)\leq\beta x+K_{\delta}, where Kδ:=δ​β/(1−δ)K_{\delta}:=\delta\beta/(1-\delta).

  2. (ii)

    At δ=1\delta=1, (58) coincides with (26): Method B deforms continuously into the undiscounted model.

  3. (iii)

    For η>0\eta>0, the fixed point satisfies Vr​sδ​(x+1)−Vr​sδ​(x)≤βV^{\delta}_{rs}(x+1)-V^{\delta}_{rs}(x)\leq\beta, the stopping region is up-closed, and a stationary threshold policy is optimal.

  4. (iv)

    For η<0\eta<0, discounting also removes the need for the robust cap: part (i) gives a finite, linearly bounded fixed point directly for the recursive criterion, and the factor δ\delta inside the exponent supplies the strict modulus. At δ=1\delta=1 the value remains finite, but the strict modulus is absent and the uncapped continuation branch lacks uniform lower control, motivating the regularized formulation of Section 2.4.

Proof of Proposition 19.

(i) For any random variables U,WU,W,

|1η​log⁡𝔼⁡[eη​δ​U]−1η​log⁡𝔼⁡[eη​δ​W]|≤δ​‖U−W‖∞.\left|\frac{1}{\eta}\log\mathbb{E}[e^{\eta\delta U}]-\frac{1}{\eta}\log\mathbb{E}[e^{\eta\delta W}]\right|\leq\delta\|U-W\|_{\infty}. (59)

Indeed, this follows by comparing UU and WW after adding ‖U−W‖∞\|U-W\|_{\infty}. On the finite grid, where the stopping branch is fixed, this gives modulus δ\delta. On ℬρ\mathcal{B}_{\rho}, the one-step bound

|u⁡(X^x)−w⁡(X^x)|≤‖u−w‖ρ​ρx+1|u(\hat{X}_{x})-w(\hat{X}_{x})|\leq\|u-w\|_{\rho}\rho^{x+1}

gives modulus δ​ρ<1\delta\rho<1. The finite one-step support also shows that the operator maps ℬρ\mathcal{B}_{\rho} into itself, so Banach’s fixed-point theorem applies.

For the linear bound, start value iteration at SS. If S≤uS\leq u and u⁡(x)≤β​x+Kδu(x)\leq\beta x+K_{\delta}, then the outer maximum preserves the lower bound, while the certainty-equivalent upper bound gives

Qr​sδ​(x)≤δ⁡[β⁡(x+1)+Kδ]−c​x≤β​x+Kδ,Q^{\delta}_{rs}(x)\leq\delta[\beta(x+1)+K_{\delta}]-cx\leq\beta x+K_{\delta},

because (1−δ)​Kδ=δ​β(1-\delta)K_{\delta}=\delta\beta. These bounds pass to the fixed point. Part (ii) is immediate.

(iii) Let η>0\eta>0. Suppose u⁡(x+1)−u⁡(x)≤βu(x+1)-u(x)\leq\beta. Using the coupling Ax+1=Ax+BA_{x+1}=A_{x}+B from Lemma 2, independence of BB and (Ax,D)(A_{x},D) gives

Δ​Qr​sδ​(x)\displaystyle\Delta Q^{\delta}_{rs}(x) ≤−c+1η​log⁡[(1−p)​eη​δ​β+p​e−η​δ​γ]\displaystyle\leq-c+\frac{1}{\eta}\log\!\left[(1-p)e^{\eta\delta\beta}+pe^{-\eta\delta\gamma}\right] (60)
=δ​β−c+1η​log⁡(1−p+p​e−η​δ​(β+γ))\displaystyle=\delta\beta-c+\frac{1}{\eta}\log\!\left(1-p+pe^{-\eta\delta(\beta+\gamma)}\right)
=δ​β−c−γ~η​δ<β,\displaystyle=\delta\beta-c-\widetilde{\gamma}_{\eta\delta}<\beta,

where

γ~η​δ:=−1η​log⁡(1−p+p​e−η​δ​(β+γ))>0.\widetilde{\gamma}_{\eta\delta}:=-\frac{1}{\eta}\log\!\left(1-p+pe^{-\eta\delta(\beta+\gamma)}\right)>0.

As in Lemma 2, the outer maximum preserves Δ​u≤β\Delta u\leq\beta, and the bound passes to Vr​sδV^{\delta}_{rs}.

To show that stopping occurs, suppose continuation were optimal everywhere and set M⁡(x):=maxy≤x⁡Vr​sδ​(y)M(x):=\max_{y\leq x}V^{\delta}_{rs}(y). For large xx,

Vr​sδ​(x)≤−c​x+M⁡(x+1).V^{\delta}_{rs}(x)\leq-cx+M(x+1).

Whenever Vr​sδ​(x+1)>M⁡(x)V^{\delta}_{rs}(x+1)>M(x), the increment bound therefore gives c​x≤βcx\leq\beta. Hence MM is eventually constant, contradicting Vr​sδ​(x)≥β​x−α→∞V^{\delta}_{rs}(x)\geq\beta x-\alpha\to\infty.

If stopping is optimal at xx, then Qr​sδ​(x)≤S⁡(x)Q^{\delta}_{rs}(x)\leq S(x), and (60) gives

Qr​sδ​(x+1)<Qr​sδ​(x)+β≤S⁡(x+1).Q^{\delta}_{rs}(x+1)<Q^{\delta}_{rs}(x)+\beta\leq S(x+1).

Thus stopping is strictly optimal at every higher state. The stopping region is consequently {x≥θ}\{x\geq\theta\} for some finite θ\theta. Policy evaluation for this threshold rule has the same δ​ρ\delta\rho-contraction, so the fixed point is attained by the corresponding first-entrance policy. Part (iv) follows directly from part (i), whose argument used no likelihood-ratio cap. ∎

The interpretation changes accordingly: (58) compounds one-period entropic risk evaluations (the recursive entropic criterion of Di Masi and Stettner, 1999, Bäuerle and Rieder, 2014), and coincides with the entropic criterion of Section 2.3.1 if and only if δ=1\delta=1.

Remark 13.

For δ<1\delta<1 the forward decomposition of Sections 2.2.3–2.3.2 is unavailable under either method: in Method A the accumulation function would need a step-dependent exponent η​δt\eta\delta^{t}, and in Method B the factor δ\delta inside the exponent destroys the linearity behind Vr​s​(x)=fr​s​(x)+const.V_{rs}(x)=f_{rs}(x)+\mathrm{const.} Both are instead solved on a truncated grid (one backward pass over the λ\lambda-grid; value iteration of a δ\delta-contraction).

Appendix B Supporting Proofs Under the Risk-Neutral Criterion

B.1 Proofs for Section 2.2

We first record the tower-property computation underlying the cost reduction of Section 2.2.1: since 𝔼⁡[At​(Xt)∣ℱt]=p​Xt\mathbb{E}[A_{t}(X_{t})\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}]=pX_{t} and {t<τ}∈ℱt\{t<\tau\}\in\mathcal{F}_{t},

𝔼x​[∑t<τδt​(c​Xt+δ​γ​At​(Xt))]=𝔼x​[∑t<τδt​(c​Xt+δ​γ​𝔼​[At​(Xt)∣ℱt])]=𝒞​𝔼x​[∑t<τδt​Xt].\mathbb{E}_{x}\Bigl[\sum_{t<\tau}\delta^{t}\bigl(cX_{t}+\delta\gamma A_{t}(X_{t})\bigr)\Bigr]=\mathbb{E}_{x}\Bigl[\sum_{t<\tau}\delta^{t}\bigl(cX_{t}+\delta\gamma\,\mathbb{E}[A_{t}(X_{t})\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}]\bigr)\Bigr]=\mathcal{C}\,\mathbb{E}_{x}\Bigl[\sum_{t<\tau}\delta^{t}X_{t}\Bigr].
Lemma 17 (Pathwise cost and reward bounds).

Define

U¯​(x):=(β+c/2)22​c−α+c2​x​(x−1),x∈ℤ+.\bar{U}(x):=\frac{(\beta+c/2)^{2}}{2c}-\alpha+\frac{c}{2}x(x-1),\qquad x\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}.

For every initial state xx and every almost surely finite stopping time τ\tau, set M:=maxt≤τ⁡XtM:=\max_{t\leq\tau}X_{t}. Then

∑t=0τ−1Xt≥M⁡(M−1)−x⁡(x−1)2\sum_{t=0}^{\tau-1}X_{t}\geq\frac{M(M-1)-x(x-1)}{2} (61)

and

ℛ1​(τ)≤K+a​M−c2​M2≤U¯​(x),\mathcal{R}_{1}(\tau)\leq K+aM-\frac{c}{2}M^{2}\leq\bar{U}(x), (62)

where

K:=−α+c2​x​(x−1),a:=β+c2.K:=-\alpha+\frac{c}{2}x(x-1),\qquad a:=\beta+\frac{c}{2}.

Moreover, if 𝔼x​[∑t<τXt]=∞\mathbb{E}_{x}[\sum_{t<\tau}X_{t}]=\infty, then 𝔼x​[ℛ1​(τ)−]=∞\mathbb{E}_{x}[\mathcal{R}_{1}(\tau)^{-}]=\infty.

Proof of Lemma 17.

By the skip-free property, every level ℓ∈{x,…,M−1}\ell\in\{x,\dots,M-1\} occurs among X0,…,Xτ−1X_{0},\dots,X_{\tau-1}, which gives (61). Since Xτ≤MX_{\tau}\leq M and abandonment penalties are nonnegative,

ℛ1​(τ)≤β​M−α−c2​[M⁡(M−1)−x⁡(x−1)]=K+a​M−c2​M2.\mathcal{R}_{1}(\tau)\leq\beta M-\alpha-\frac{c}{2}\bigl[M(M-1)-x(x-1)\bigr]=K+aM-\frac{c}{2}M^{2}.

Maximizing the concave quadratic over M≥0M\geq 0 gives (62).

To prove the final assertion, we establish the contrapositive. Define the total running cost

Cτ:=∑t=0τ−1(c​Xt+γ​At​(Xt)),so thatℛ1​(τ)=β​Xτ−α−Cτ.C_{\tau}:=\sum_{t=0}^{\tau-1}\bigl(cX_{t}+\gamma A_{t}(X_{t})\bigr),\qquad\text{so that}\qquad\mathcal{R}_{1}(\tau)=\beta X_{\tau}-\alpha-C_{\tau}.

Suppose that 𝔼x​[ℛ1​(τ)−]<∞\mathbb{E}_{x}[\mathcal{R}_{1}(\tau)^{-}]<\infty. Because (62) also bounds ℛ1​(τ)\mathcal{R}_{1}(\tau) above by the finite deterministic constant U¯​(x)\bar{U}(x), the positive part ℛ1​(τ)+\mathcal{R}_{1}(\tau)^{+} is bounded, and hence ℛ1​(τ)\mathcal{R}_{1}(\tau) is integrable. Moreover, the first inequality in (62) gives

ℛ1​(τ)−≥(c2​M2−a​M−K)+.\mathcal{R}_{1}(\tau)^{-}\geq\left(\frac{c}{2}M^{2}-aM-K\right)^{+}.

Integrability of the left-hand side therefore implies 𝔼x​[M2]<∞\mathbb{E}_{x}[M^{2}]<\infty; otherwise, the positive quadratic expression on the right-hand side would have infinite expectation. Consequently, 𝔼x​[M]<∞\mathbb{E}_{x}[M]<\infty, and since Xτ≤MX_{\tau}\leq M, the terminal reward β​Xτ−α\beta X_{\tau}-\alpha is integrable. It now follows from

Cτ=β​Xτ−α−ℛ1​(τ)C_{\tau}=\beta X_{\tau}-\alpha-\mathcal{R}_{1}(\tau)

that 𝔼x​[Cτ]<∞\mathbb{E}_{x}[C_{\tau}]<\infty. Finally, Cτ≥c​∑t<τXtC_{\tau}\geq c\sum_{t<\tau}X_{t}, so

𝔼x​[∑t<τXt]≤1c​𝔼x​[Cτ]<∞.\mathbb{E}_{x}\!\left[\sum_{t<\tau}X_{t}\right]\leq\frac{1}{c}\,\mathbb{E}_{x}[C_{\tau}]<\infty.

Thus, if 𝔼x​[∑t<τXt]=∞\mathbb{E}_{x}[\sum_{t<\tau}X_{t}]=\infty, then 𝔼x​[ℛ1​(τ)−]=∞\mathbb{E}_{x}[\mathcal{R}_{1}(\tau)^{-}]=\infty. □\Box ∎

𝔼⁡[ρX^x]=ρx​(1−p+p​ρ−1)x​(1−q+q​ρ)≤ρx​(1−q+q​ρ),\mathbb{E}[\rho^{\hat{X}_{x}}]=\rho^{x}(1-p+p\rho^{-1})^{x}(1-q+q\rho)\leq\rho^{x}(1-q+q\rho),

−𝒞​x+δ​𝔼​[V^​(X^x)]=U⁡(x)=V^​(x)>S⁡(x),-\mathcal{C}x+\delta\,\mathbb{E}[\widehat{V}(\hat{X}_{x})]=U(x)=\widehat{V}(x)>S(x),

so continuation is optimal at xx.

For x≥θ∗x\geq\theta^{*}, define the stopping advantage

Λ⁡(x):=S⁡(x)+𝒞​x−δ​𝔼​[V^​(X^x)].\Lambda(x):=S(x)+\mathcal{C}x-\delta\,\mathbb{E}[\widehat{V}(\hat{X}_{x})].

Stopping is optimal at xx exactly when Λ⁡(x)≥0\Lambda(x)\geq 0. Using (65),

Λ(x)=δ𝔼[h(X^x)𝟏{X^x>θ∗}]−h(x).\Lambda(x)=\delta\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[h(\hat{X}_{x})\mathbf{1}_{\{\hat{X}_{x}>\theta^{*}\}}\right]-h(x).

At x=θ∗x=\theta^{*}, only the event X^θ∗=θ∗+1\hat{X}_{\theta^{*}}=\theta^{*}+1 contributes, so

Λ⁡(θ∗)\displaystyle\Lambda(\theta^{*}) =δ​q​(1−p)θ∗​h​(θ∗+1)=−δ​q​(1−p)θ∗​g​(θ∗+1)​Δ​vr​n​(θ∗)≥0.\displaystyle=\delta q(1-p)^{\theta^{*}}h(\theta^{*}+1)=-\delta q(1-p)^{\theta^{*}}g(\theta^{*}+1)\Delta v_{rn}(\theta^{*})\geq 0. (66)

For monotonicity, write instead

Λ(x)=μ(x)−δ𝔼[h(X^x)𝟏{X^x≤θ∗}],μ(x):=S(x)+𝒞x−δ𝔼[S(X^x)].\Lambda(x)=\mu(x)-\delta\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[h(\hat{X}_{x})\mathbf{1}_{\{\hat{X}_{x}\leq\theta^{*}\}}\right],\qquad\mu(x):=S(x)+\mathcal{C}x-\delta\,\mathbb{E}[S(\hat{X}_{x})].

Since 𝔼⁡[X^x]=(1−p)​x+q\mathbb{E}[\hat{X}_{x}]=(1-p)x+q, μ⁡(x)=[β⁡(1−δ⁡(1−p))+𝒞]​x−δ​β​q−(1−δ)​α\mu(x)=\bigl[\beta(1-\delta(1-p))+\mathcal{C}\bigr]x-\delta\beta q-(1-\delta)\alpha is strictly increasing. Moreover, coupling Ax+1=Ax+BA_{x+1}=A_{x}+B, with B∼Bernoulli⁡(p)B\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p), gives X^x+1=X^x+1−B≥X^x\hat{X}_{x+1}=\hat{X}_{x}+1-B\geq\hat{X}_{x}, and because hh is decreasing below θ∗\theta^{*}, the expected lower-tail term is nonincreasing in xx. Hence Λ\Lambda is nondecreasing on x≥θ∗x\geq\theta^{*}, and (66) implies Λ⁡(x)≥0\Lambda(x)\geq 0.

Thus continuation is optimal below θ∗\theta^{*}, stopping is optimal from θ∗\theta^{*} upward, and V^\widehat{V} solves (9). ∎

Since z↦e−η​zz\mapsto e^{-\eta z} is strictly decreasing, 𝔼⁡[e−η​CU]≤e−η​c​𝔼​[e−η​CL]\mathbb{E}[e^{-\eta C^{U}}]\leq e^{-\eta c}\,\mathbb{E}[e^{-\eta C^{L}}], and applying −η−1​log-\eta^{-1}\log gives Δ​fr​s​(θ+1)≥Δ​fr​s​(θ)+c\Delta f_{rs}(\theta+1)\geq\Delta f_{rs}(\theta)+c, i.e., Δ2​fr​s​(θ)≥c\Delta^{2}f_{rs}(\theta)\geq c. The remaining claims follow from Δ​fr​s​(0)=0\Delta f_{rs}(0)=0 by telescoping. ∎

Appendix E Proof of Proposition 8

Proof of Proposition 8.

(i) Proposition 13(iii) gives θr​s,η∗≥θr​n∗\theta^{*}_{rs,\eta}\geq\theta^{*}_{rn}. For the risk-averse problem, 𝒯r​a,η′≤𝒯r​n\mathcal{T}_{ra,\eta^{\prime}}\leq\mathcal{T}_{rn} by (54). Value iteration from SS therefore gives S≤Vr​a,η′≤Vr​nS\leq V_{ra,\eta^{\prime}}\leq V_{rn}. Consequently, every risk-neutral stopping state is also risk-averse stopping state, and taking minima gives θr​a,η′∗≤θr​n∗\theta^{*}_{ra,\eta^{\prime}}\leq\theta^{*}_{rn}.

(ii) Risk-seeking limit. From any y<θy<\theta, the probability of reaching θ\theta within θ\theta steps is at least (q​(1−p)θ−1)θ\bigl(q(1-p)^{\theta-1}\bigr)^{\theta}. The usual block argument therefore gives geometric hitting-time tails and finite local exponential moments for every excursion cost. Hence the cumulant expansions used below are valid.

By (68) and (51), Hölder’s inequality shows that fr​s,η​(θ)f_{rs,\eta}(\theta) and Δ​fr​s,η​(θ)\Delta f_{rs,\eta}(\theta) are nonincreasing in η>0\eta>0, while expansion at η=0\eta=0 gives

fr​s,η(θ)↑f(θ),Δfr​s,η(θ)↑Δf(θ)(η↓0).f_{rs,\eta}(\theta)\uparrow f(\theta),\qquad\Delta f_{rs,\eta}(\theta)\uparrow\Delta f(\theta)\qquad(\eta\downarrow 0).

Thus vr​s,η​(θ)↓vr​n​(θ)v_{rs,\eta}(\theta)\downarrow v_{rn}(\theta) pointwise. Both maximizations are effectively over Θ¯:={0,…,⌈β/c⌉}\bar{\Theta}:=\{0,\dots,\lceil\beta/c\rceil\}: the risk-seeking bound is in Theorem 2(ii), and the risk-neutral bound follows from Δ​f​(θ)≥c​θ\Delta f(\theta)\geq c\theta. Convergence of maxima over this finite set gives

Vr​s,η​(0)↓Vr​n​(0).V_{rs,\eta}(0)\downarrow V_{rn}(0). (75)

Next, Δ​f​(0)=0<β\Delta f(0)=0<\beta, so θr​n∗≥1\theta^{*}_{rn}\geq 1. For every θ≥1\theta\geq 1, the excursion cost is nondegenerate and strict Jensen gives Δ​fr​s,η​(θ)<Δ​f​(θ)\Delta f_{rs,\eta}(\theta)<\Delta f(\theta). In the unique risk-neutral maximizer case, Δ​f​(θr​n∗)>β\Delta f(\theta^{*}_{rn})>\beta, so convergence yields θr​s,η∗=θr​n∗\theta^{*}_{rs,\eta}=\theta^{*}_{rn} eventually. In the tie case, strict Jensen at θr​n∗\theta^{*}_{rn} and convergence at θr​n∗+1\theta^{*}_{rn}+1 instead give θr​s,η∗=θr​n∗+1\theta^{*}_{rs,\eta}=\theta^{*}_{rn}+1 eventually.

Operator-level Lyapunov monotonicity and value iteration from SS show that Vr​s,η​(x)V_{rs,\eta}(x) is nondecreasing in η\eta. The additive decomposition and the eventual threshold stabilization now give pointwise convergence: if x<θr​n∗x<\theta^{*}_{rn}, then eventually

Vr​s,η​(x)=fr​s,η​(x)+Vr​s,η​(0)↓f⁡(x)+Vr​n​(0)=Vr​n​(x).V_{rs,\eta}(x)=f_{rs,\eta}(x)+V_{rs,\eta}(0)\downarrow f(x)+V_{rn}(0)=V_{rn}(x).

At x=θr​n∗x=\theta^{*}_{rn}, either the same display applies or both values equal S⁡(x)S(x). If x>θr​n∗x>\theta^{*}_{rn}, then eventually x≥θr​s,η∗x\geq\theta^{*}_{rs,\eta}, so Vr​s,η​(x)=S⁡(x)=Vr​n​(x)V_{rs,\eta}(x)=S(x)=V_{rn}(x).

(iii) Risk-averse limit. Set kη:=−1/ηk_{\eta}:=-1/\eta. For bounded ZZ, define

ℛη,x(Z):=infℚx∈𝒬κ​(x){𝔼ℚx[Z]+kηDKL(ℚx∥ℙx)}.\mathcal{R}_{\eta,x}(Z):=\inf_{\mathbb{Q}_{x}\in\mathcal{Q}_{\kappa}(x)}\left\{\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}_{x}}[Z]+k_{\eta}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathbb{Q}_{x}\|\mathbb{P}_{x})\right\}.

Comparing the capped and uncapped infima and evaluating at the nominal measure gives

Both sides converge to 𝔼ℙx​[Z]\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{x}}[Z] as η↑0\eta\uparrow 0, and monotonicity follows from the increasing KL multiplier. Hence ℛη,x​(Z)↑𝔼ℙx​[Z]\mathcal{R}_{\eta,x}(Z)\uparrow\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{x}}[Z].

The corresponding value functions increase to some V∗≤Vr​nV^{*}\leq V_{rn}. On each finite one-step support, the uniform bound

Finally, part (i) gives θr​a,η∗≤θr​n∗\theta^{*}_{ra,\eta}\leq\theta^{*}_{rn}. Since

ξ1(θ):=Δ​N1​(θ)Δ​t​(θ),ξδ(θ):=Δ​Nδ​(θ)Δ​g​(θ,δ)(δ∈(0,1)).\xi_{1}(\theta):=\frac{\Delta N_{1}(\theta)}{\Delta t(\theta)},\qquad\xi_{\delta}(\theta):=\frac{\Delta N_{\delta}(\theta)}{\Delta g(\theta;\delta)}\quad(\delta\in(0,1)). (77)

Both denominators are strictly positive by Lemma 18, and

ξ1​(θ)=β+𝒞1/pΔ​t​(θ)−𝒞1​qp,ξδ​(θ)=β+c¯Δ​g​(θ,δ)−C∞.\xi_{1}(\theta)=\frac{\beta+\mathcal{C}_{1}/p}{\Delta t(\theta)}-\frac{\mathcal{C}_{1}q}{p},\qquad\xi_{\delta}(\theta)=\frac{\beta+\bar{c}}{\Delta g(\theta;\delta)}-C_{\infty}. (78)

Appendix G Computational Algorithms

G.1 Forward-Recursive Threshold Algorithms

The risk-neutral, risk-seeking, and repeated-clearing problems admit the same forward-ascent implementation. For each regime jj, let 𝒜j\mathcal{A}_{j} denote its accumulation sequences and vjv_{j} its reduced objective, as specified in Table 3. Starting from the indicated initial index xjx_{j}, the recurrences are extended one state at a time. Theorems 1, 2, and 4 imply that the first nonpositive increment of vjv_{j} identifies the smallest optimal threshold; in the equality case, the adjacent threshold x+1x+1 is also optimal.

Each transition-weighted sum at state xx requires 𝒪⁡(x)\mathcal{O}(x) operations. Consequently, every case in Table 3 uses 𝒪⁡((θj∗)2)\mathcal{O}((\theta_{j}^{*})^{2}) time and 𝒪⁡(θj∗)\mathcal{O}(\theta_{j}^{*}) space. Finite termination follows from the corresponding optimality theorem; additionally, θr​s∗≤⌈β/c⌉\theta_{rs}^{*}\leq\lceil\beta/c\rceil. At δ=1\delta=1, set g≡1g\equiv 1 directly rather than evaluating its numerically sensitive recursion.

G.2 Computational Algorithm for the Risk-Averse Problem

For the regularized risk-averse problem (η<0\eta<0, δ=1\delta=1), no forward recursion is available; we solve (37) by value iteration from V0=SV_{0}=S, which increases pointwise to Vr​aκV_{ra}^{\kappa} (Theorem 3(i)). Proposition 8 provides an exact truncation: imposing stopping at Xmax=θr​n∗X_{\max}=\theta^{*}_{rn} leaves the solution unchanged on {0,…,Xmax}\{0,\dots,X_{\max}\}.

At each state xx, the continuation value requires the worst-case distortion ℚx∗∈𝒬κ​(x)\mathbb{Q}_{x}^{*}\in\mathcal{Q}_{\kappa}(x) of the joint law ℙx\mathbb{P}_{x} over (a,d)∈{0,…,x}×{0,1}(a,d)\in\{0,\dots,x\}\times\{0,1\}. By Theorem 3(iii), the likelihood ratio is the truncated tilt m∗​(a,d)=min⁡(κ,λx​eη​φ​(a,d))m^{*}(a,d)=\min\bigl(\kappa,\lambda_{x}e^{\eta\varphi(a,d)}\bigr) with φ⁡(a,d)=Vr​aκ​(x−a+d)−γ​a\varphi(a,d)=V_{ra}^{\kappa}(x-a+d)-\gamma a, so the variational problem reduces to the scalar equation

∑a=0x∑d=01ℙx​(a,d)​min⁡(κ,λx​eη​φ​(a,d))=1,\sum_{a=0}^{x}\sum_{d=0}^{1}\mathbb{P}_{x}(a,d)\,\min\bigl(\kappa,\,\lambda_{x}e^{\eta\varphi(a,d)}\bigr)=1,

whose left-hand side is continuous in λx\lambda_{x}, increases from 00 to κ>1\kappa>1, and is strictly increasing at the root; we locate log⁡λx\log\lambda_{x} by bisection over an adaptively expanded bracket.

Computational complexity. Each sweep costs 𝒪⁡(Xmax2)\mathcal{O}(X_{\max}^{2}) operations (2​(x+1)2(x+1) atoms per state; bisection contributes a constant factor) and 𝒪⁡(Xmax)\mathcal{O}(X_{\max}) memory. At the baseline calibration, convergence to ε=10−8\varepsilon=10^{-8} requires on the order of 10310^{3} sweeps, reducible tenfold by warm-starting from a nearby parameter value.

Appendix H Theoretical Sensitivity Results

This section develops the comparative statics of the optimal risk-neutral threshold θr​n∗\theta^{*}_{rn} of Theorem 1: Lemma 21 covers the cost parameters (c,γ)(c,\gamma) and α\alpha; the remaining results concern the interaction of β\beta with δ\delta, governed by the sign of a single phase function. Throughout, ff and gg are the accumulation functions of Section 2.2.3; we write g⁡(θ,δ)g(\theta;\delta) when the dependence on δ\delta matters.

Lemma 21.

Let θr​n∗\theta^{*}_{rn} be the optimal risk-neutral threshold characterized in Theorem 1, and fix all other primitives.

  1. (i)

    θr​n∗\theta^{*}_{rn} is nonincreasing in each of the cost parameters cc and γ\gamma.

  2. (ii)

    For δ<1\delta<1, θr​n∗\theta^{*}_{rn} is nondecreasing in α\alpha. For δ=1\delta=1, vr​n​(θ)=β​θ−α−f⁡(θ)v_{rn}(\theta)=\beta\theta-\alpha-f(\theta), so α\alpha shifts the objective by a constant and θr​n∗\theta^{*}_{rn} is independent of α\alpha.

𝒯c,γ​V​(x)=max⁡{S⁡(x),−c​x−δ​γ​p​x+δ​𝔼ℙx​[V⁡(X^x)]}.\mathcal{T}_{c,\gamma}V(x)=\max\!\left\{S(x),\,-cx-\delta\gamma px+\delta\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{x}}[V(\hat{X}_{x})]\right\}.

Vr​n​(⋅,c′,γ′)≤Vr​n​(⋅,c,γ)componentwise.V_{rn}(\cdot\,;c^{\prime},\gamma^{\prime})\leq V_{rn}(\cdot\,;c,\gamma)\qquad\text{componentwise.}

By Theorem 1(iii), the optimal stopping region is

𝒮∗​(c,γ)={θr​n∗​(c,γ),θr​n∗​(c,γ)+1,…}.\mathcal{S}^{*}(c,\gamma)=\{\theta^{*}_{rn}(c,\gamma),\theta^{*}_{rn}(c,\gamma)+1,\dots\}.

and hence θr​n∗​(c′,γ′)≤θr​n∗​(c,γ)\theta^{*}_{rn}(c^{\prime},\gamma^{\prime})\leq\theta^{*}_{rn}(c,\gamma).

(ii) For δ<1\delta<1, Proposition 3 gives

vr​n​(θ,α)=β​θ−α−f⁡(θ)g⁡(θ),v_{rn}(\theta;\alpha)=\frac{\beta\theta-\alpha-f(\theta)}{g(\theta)},

vr​n​(θ,α2)−vr​n​(θ1,α2)\displaystyle v_{rn}(\theta;\alpha_{2})-v_{rn}(\theta_{1};\alpha_{2})
=[vr​n​(θ,α1)−vr​n​(θ1,α1)]+(α2−α1)​(1g⁡(θ1)−1g⁡(θ))<0.\displaystyle=\bigl[v_{rn}(\theta;\alpha_{1})-v_{rn}(\theta_{1};\alpha_{1})\bigr]+(\alpha_{2}-\alpha_{1})\left(\frac{1}{g(\theta_{1})}-\frac{1}{g(\theta)}\right)<0.

Remark 14 (The probability parameters pp and qq).

Varying pp or qq changes the transition kernel itself rather than a one-step cost, so the operator comparison above does not apply. The directions reported in Section 4.2—θr​n∗\theta^{*}_{rn} nonincreasing in pp and nondecreasing in qq on the computed grid (Figure 1)—are therefore numerical observations; an analytic proof remains open.

The next lemma records the only discount-monotonicity statement needed below.

Lemma 22 (Discount monotonicity of the accumulation ratio).

For each x≥0x\geq 0, the ratio δ↦g⁡(x+1,δ)/g⁡(x,δ)\delta\mapsto g(x+1;\delta)/g(x;\delta) is strictly decreasing on (0,1](0,1].

Proof of Lemma 22.

By Remark 2, 1/g⁡(x,δ)=𝔼0​[δTx]1/g(x;\delta)=\mathbb{E}_{0}[\delta^{T_{x}}] with Tx:=min⁡{t≥0:Xt=x}T_{x}:=\min\{t\geq 0:X_{t}=x\}. Since the chain is skip-free to the right (Lemma 1), reaching x+1x+1 requires first reaching xx, so the strong Markov property gives

(the excursion analogue of TxT_{x}). Since Tx→x+1≥1T_{x\to x+1}\geq 1 almost surely and ℙx​(Tx→x+1=1)=(1−p)x​q>0\mathbb{P}_{x}(T_{x\to x+1}=1)=(1-p)^{x}q>0, the map 𝔼x​[δTx→x+1]=∑k≥1δk​ℙx​(Tx→x+1=k)\mathbb{E}_{x}[\delta^{T_{x\to x+1}}]=\sum_{k\geq 1}\delta^{k}\,\mathbb{P}_{x}(T_{x\to x+1}=k) is a power series in δ\delta with nonnegative coefficients and a positive leading coefficient; it is strictly increasing on (0,1](0,1], and its reciprocal is strictly decreasing. ∎

We turn to the interaction of β\beta and δ\delta. The β\beta-dependent part of vr​n​(θ)=(β​θ−α−f⁡(θ))/g⁡(θ,δ)v_{rn}(\theta)=\bigl(\beta\theta-\alpha-f(\theta)\bigr)/g(\theta;\delta) is β​θ/g⁡(θ,δ)\beta\,\theta/g(\theta;\delta), so the comparative statics of θr​n∗\theta^{*}_{rn} in β\beta are governed by the increment

Φ⁡(θ,δ):=Δ⁡[θg⁡(θ,δ)]=θ+1g⁡(θ+1,δ)−θg⁡(θ,δ),\Phi(\theta;\delta)\;:=\;\Delta\!\left[\frac{\theta}{g(\theta;\delta)}\right]=\frac{\theta+1}{g(\theta+1;\delta)}-\frac{\theta}{g(\theta;\delta)},

which we call the phase function; it depends neither on β\beta nor on the cost parameters.

Proposition 20 (Sign structure of the phase function).

For each θ≥1\theta\geq 1, the following hold.

  1. (i)

    (Factorization) With Tθ→θ+1T_{\theta\to\theta+1} as above,

    Φ⁡(θ,δ)=𝔼0​[δTθ]​((θ+1)​𝔼θ​[δTθ→θ+1]−θ);\Phi(\theta;\delta)=\mathbb{E}_{0}\bigl[\delta^{T_{\theta}}\bigr]\,\Bigl((\theta+1)\,\mathbb{E}_{\theta}\bigl[\delta^{T_{\theta\to\theta+1}}\bigr]-\theta\Bigr);

    the first factor is positive, so Φ⁡(θ,δ)\Phi(\theta;\delta) has the sign of the bracketed term. Moreover, Φ⁡(θ,⋅)\Phi(\theta;\cdot) is continuous on (0,1](0,1], with Φ⁡(θ,1)=1\Phi(\theta;1)=1.

  2. (ii)

    (Low discount factors) Φ⁡(θ,δ)<0\Phi(\theta;\delta)<0 whenever δ<θ/(θ+1)\delta<\theta/(\theta+1); in particular, Φ⁡(θ,δ)<0\Phi(\theta;\delta)<0 for all θ≥1\theta\geq 1 whenever δ<1/2\delta<1/2.

  3. (iii)

    (Phase boundary) Φ⁡(θ,⋅)\Phi(\theta;\cdot) has exactly one zero δθ\delta_{\theta} in (0,1)(0,1), with Φ⁡(θ,δ)<0\Phi(\theta;\delta)<0 for δ<δθ\delta<\delta_{\theta} and Φ⁡(θ,δ)>0\Phi(\theta;\delta)>0 for δ>δθ\delta>\delta_{\theta}. Moreover, δθ≥θ/(θ+1)\delta_{\theta}\geq\theta/(\theta+1); in particular, δθ→1\delta_{\theta}\to 1 as θ→∞\theta\to\infty, and for every fixed δ<1\delta<1 all θ>δ/(1−δ)\theta>\delta/(1-\delta) have Φ⁡(θ,δ)<0\Phi(\theta;\delta)<0.

Proof of Proposition 20.

(i) By Remark 2 and the strong Markov property for the skip-free chain (Lemma 1), 𝔼0​[δTθ+1]=𝔼0​[δTθ]​𝔼θ​[δTθ→θ+1]\mathbb{E}_{0}[\delta^{T_{\theta+1}}]=\mathbb{E}_{0}[\delta^{T_{\theta}}]\,\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[\delta^{T_{\theta\to\theta+1}}]; substituting 1/g⁡(x,δ)=𝔼0​[δTx]1/g(x;\delta)=\mathbb{E}_{0}[\delta^{T_{x}}] into the definition of Φ\Phi gives the desired identity, and 𝔼0​[δTθ]>0\mathbb{E}_{0}[\delta^{T_{\theta}}]>0. Each factor is a power series in δ\delta with nonnegative coefficients, hence continuous on (0,1](0,1]. (ii) Since Tθ→θ+1≥1T_{\theta\to\theta+1}\geq 1 almost surely, 𝔼θ​[δTθ→θ+1]≤δ\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[\delta^{T_{\theta\to\theta+1}}]\leq\delta, so the bracket in part (i) is at most (θ+1)​δ−θ<0(\theta+1)\delta-\theta<0 whenever δ<θ/(θ+1)\delta<\theta/(\theta+1); the uniform claim follows because θ/(θ+1)≥1/2\theta/(\theta+1)\geq 1/2 for all θ≥1\theta\geq 1.

Hence Φ⁡(θ,⋅)\Phi(\theta;\cdot) has exactly one zero δθ∈[θ/(θ+1),1)\delta_{\theta}\in[\theta/(\theta+1),1), and the sign claims follow from strict monotonicity; the final claims follow because δ<θ/(θ+1)\delta<\theta/(\theta+1) is equivalent to θ>δ/(1−δ)\theta>\delta/(1-\delta). ∎

Corollary 2 (Comparative statics in the per-item reward).

Fix (c,γ,α)(c,\gamma,\alpha) and δ\delta, and write θr​n∗​(β)\theta^{*}_{rn}(\beta) for the optimal threshold of Theorem 1 as a function of β\beta.

  1. (i)

    If Φ⁡(θ,δ)≤0\Phi(\theta;\delta)\leq 0 for all θ≥θr​n∗​(β1)\theta\geq\theta^{*}_{rn}(\beta_{1})—in particular, if δ<1/2\delta<1/2—then θr​n∗​(β2)≤θr​n∗​(β1)\theta^{*}_{rn}(\beta_{2})\leq\theta^{*}_{rn}(\beta_{1}) for all β2>β1\beta_{2}>\beta_{1}.

  2. (ii)

    If Φ⁡(θ,δ)≥0\Phi(\theta;\delta)\geq 0 for all θ≤θr​n∗​(β1)\theta\leq\theta^{*}_{rn}(\beta_{1}), then θr​n∗​(β2)≥θr​n∗​(β1)\theta^{*}_{rn}(\beta_{2})\geq\theta^{*}_{rn}(\beta_{1}) for all β2>β1\beta_{2}>\beta_{1}.

Proof of Corollary 2.

The reduced objective is affine in β\beta: vr​n​(θ,β)=(β​θ−α−f⁡(θ))/g⁡(θ,δ)v_{rn}(\theta;\beta)=\bigl(\beta\theta-\alpha-f(\theta)\bigr)/g(\theta;\delta) (with g≡1g\equiv 1 when δ=1\delta=1), with ff and gg independent of β\beta (Proposition 3). Hence, for β2>β1\beta_{2}>\beta_{1} and θ1:=θr​n∗​(β1)\theta_{1}:=\theta^{*}_{rn}(\beta_{1}),

vr​n​(θ,β2)−vr​n​(θ1,β2)=[vr​n​(θ,β1)−vr​n​(θ1,β1)]+(β2−β1)​(θg⁡(θ,δ)−θ1g⁡(θ1,δ)).v_{rn}(\theta;\beta_{2})-v_{rn}(\theta_{1};\beta_{2})=\bigl[v_{rn}(\theta;\beta_{1})-v_{rn}(\theta_{1};\beta_{1})\bigr]+(\beta_{2}-\beta_{1})\Bigl(\frac{\theta}{g(\theta;\delta)}-\frac{\theta_{1}}{g(\theta_{1};\delta)}\Bigr).

Hence the smallest maximizer of vr​n​(⋅,β2)v_{rn}(\cdot\,;\beta_{2}) is at most θ1\theta_{1}.

(ii) For any θ<θ1\theta<\theta_{1}, the first bracket is strictly negative because θ1\theta_{1} is the smallest maximizer and vr​n​(⋅,β1)v_{rn}(\cdot\,;\beta_{1}) is strictly increasing on {0,…,θ1}\{0,\dots,\theta_{1}\} (Theorem 1(i)), and the second term is nonpositive because θ↦θ/g⁡(θ,δ)\theta\mapsto\theta/g(\theta;\delta) is nondecreasing on {0,…,θ1}\{0,\dots,\theta_{1}\} by hypothesis. Hence no θ<θ1\theta<\theta_{1} maximizes vr​n​(⋅,β2)v_{rn}(\cdot\,;\beta_{2}), so θr​n∗​(β2)≥θ1\theta^{*}_{rn}(\beta_{2})\geq\theta_{1}. ∎

Remark 15.

At δ=1\delta=1, Φ⁡(θ,1)=1\Phi(\theta;1)=1 (Proposition 20(i)), so Corollary 2(ii) applies without restriction: θr​n∗\theta^{*}_{rn} is nondecreasing in β\beta when δ=1\delta=1.

H.1 Reward–Discount Phase Transition

By Corollary 2, the sign of Φ⁡(θ,δ)\Phi(\theta;\delta) determines how θr​n∗\theta^{*}_{rn} responds to β\beta: nonincreasing where Φ<0\Phi<0, nondecreasing where Φ>0\Phi>0. Since Φ\Phi depends on neither β\beta nor the cost parameters, the (θ,δ)(\theta,\delta) plane is partitioned by its zero set; by Proposition 20(iii) the zero δθ\delta_{\theta} is unique, lies in [θ/(θ+1),1)[\theta/(\theta+1),1), and converges to 11. In all our experiments, δθ\delta_{\theta} is increasing in θ\theta, so Φ⁡(θ,δ)>0\Phi(\theta;\delta)>0 exactly for θ<θ¯​(δ):=min⁡{θ:δθ≥δ}\theta<\bar{\theta}(\delta):=\min\{\theta:\delta_{\theta}\geq\delta\}, and the conditions of Corollary 2 reduce to comparing θr​n∗\theta^{*}_{rn} with θ¯​(δ)\bar{\theta}(\delta).

Figure 6(a) displays the boundary δθ\delta_{\theta} (log scale in 1−δ1-\delta) for q=0.8q=0.8 and p∈{0.005,0.01,0.02}p\in\{0.005,0.01,0.02\}. It rises toward 11 as θ\theta grows, in line with δθ≥θ/(θ+1)\delta_{\theta}\geq\theta/(\theta+1) (δ1≈0.56\delta_{1}\approx 0.56, versus 1/21/2; δ43=0.9865,0.9913,0.9991\delta_{43}=0.9865,0.9913,0.9991 for the three values of pp, versus 43/44≈0.97743/44\approx 0.977), and moves up as pp increases. Economically, β​Φ​(θ,δ)\beta\,\Phi(\theta;\delta) is the marginal discounted-reward content of one additional item: in the sign-negative region, waiting for a larger batch discounts the per-item reward more heavily than the batch size grows, so a higher β\beta weakly lowers the threshold.

Figure 6(b) redraws the boundary in the (β,δ)(\beta,\delta) plane for p=0.01p=0.01 and q∈{0.6,0.8,1.0}q\in\{0.6,0.8,1.0\} (q=1q=1 being the deterministic-arrival limit), tracing where θr​n∗​(β)\theta^{*}_{rn}(\beta)—recomputed at each grid point—coincides with θ¯​(δ)\bar{\theta}(\delta). The boundary decreases slightly as qq rises, with visibly smaller sensitivity to qq than to pp in panel (a).
